# Session module

This page explains how `src/game/session` connects the pure game model to React, browser lifecycle and saved preferences.

The directory contains both pure transformations and browser adapters. `session.ts` can be called without React; `use-game.ts` provides a controller for components; the clock and storage hooks perform effects. Keeping those roles distinct makes it possible to explain a click as a sequence of ordinary data decisions followed by rendering and persistence.

## The Session value

`Session` contains eight fields. `game` is the complete `GameState`. `paused` gates an imported unfinished game. `generation` identifies replacement lifetimes. `feedback` is the current published result or notice. `loadNotice` retains load-related text for the reproduction controls. `announcement` distinguishes feedback events. `celebration` records whether this session just completed through play. `preferences` contains selected size and best moves.

These fields are not redundant copies of the core. `isWon(game)` derives victory from matched positions; there is no second `won` boolean in the session. `celebration` answers a different question from victory: a completed import is won but has no new-completion treatment. `paused` likewise describes how the browser entered the game, not whether the snapshot describes a legal state.

The game formats serialize game progress, not the whole session. A generation, browser pause, draft form text or feedback event does not appear in an exported snapshot. This lets the same snapshot be reconstructed in another session without carrying browser bookkeeping into the core model.

## Initialization

`initialSession(code, preferences)` creates a game with `createGame`. It initializes `paused` and `celebration` to false, `generation` and `announcement` to zero and both message fields to empty strings. It retains the supplied preferences.

The React controller obtains its browser store once through a lazy `useState(browserStore)`. A second lazy state initializer reads preferences, requests a fresh board for the valid saved size and calls `initialSession`. The first board therefore depends on the saved size but not on an automatically restored progress record. Active progress remains in memory until explicitly exchanged through a snapshot.

`browserStore` catches failure while obtaining `window.localStorage` and returns `null` if access is blocked. `readPreferences` can use that null store and return the default. Initialization is consequently resilient to the storage access failure that browsers can raise before `getItem` is even called.

## The current ref and React state

`useGame` maintains both React's `session` value and a `current` ref. Its `commit(next)` first compares object identity. If nothing changed it returns. Otherwise it updates the ref and then calls `setSession(next)`.

This order gives event handlers and timer callbacks immediate access to the latest committed session even before React has rendered it. Several operations can happen in a single browser task. Reading only the session captured by the last render could make an export or subsequent activation use an older game.

The ref is not an independent state machine. Every change still passes through the same commit operation, and React renders the corresponding state. The clock hook receives the ref and commit function so it can apply deltas to current data rather than a stale closure. [React boundaries](react-boundaries.md) follows the component consequences.

## Card activation

The exposed `activate(index)` synchronizes the clock, then commits `activateSession(current.current, index)`. Synchronization can close an overdue mismatch before the core decides whether the new activation is allowed. It also accounts for the interval before a final winning match.

`activateSession` rejects input while paused. It calls `activateCard` and returns the same session if the game is unchanged. For a first reveal, whose resulting selection is `one`, it returns a session with only the new game. There is no completed-turn message yet.

For a completed attempt, it derives victory and chooses feedback. A mismatch reports that the cards will close after a short pause. A match reports the matched pair count with singular/plural wording. A final match combines the pair result with the total moves and formatted elapsed time. The function increments `announcement` once for that turn.

A winning activation calls `rememberBest`, and `celebration` becomes true. The source implements direct game-derived transitions rather than a separate event bus.

## Why feedback has an event counter

Two consecutive mismatch attempts can produce identical text. A string comparison alone would make them look like the same event. The session counter gives `Game.tsx` a changing key for the span containing the text, so repeated outcomes remain distinct render events.

A first reveal does not increment the counter. A timer closing a mismatch does not increment it either: `tickSession` changes the game, while the turn result remains the same feedback. A new deal clears the text silently without incrementing the counter. Imports increment it to publish the load notice.

`loadNotice` serves the reproduction area separately from turn feedback. It is populated by imports and invalid load attempts and cleared on replacement without import or on Resume. A later turn result can change `feedback` without treating ordinary play as a new load message.

## Replacing a game

`replaceGame(session, game, imported)` preserves the surrounding session, installs the supplied game and increments generation. It sets the saved size to the new game's size, clears celebration and computes import pause and notices.

If `imported` is false, the replacement is unpaused, its load notice is empty and the last turn feedback is cleared. If true and unfinished, the session is paused with the loaded-snapshot notice. If true and already won, it is unpaused with the completed-snapshot notice. The latter is a static completed state rather than a completion event through activation.

A replacement does not itself call `rememberBest`. This matters for completed imports, whose supplied moves are not treated as a newly played local result. Finishing an unfinished imported game through activations does reach the ordinary completion path and can record its resulting best moves.

The generation increment has two consumers. Timer logic can reject work associated with an earlier game, and `Game.tsx` uses it to remount the board. `BoardCodeForm` also keys the input by generation so a replacement supplies a fresh current-code value. A restart of the same code still gets a new lifetime.

## Controller actions

| Controller action | Validation or preparation | Session effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `newGame(size?)` | Validate size, choose a fresh code excluding the current seed, reset clock | Replace with a new initial game |
| `restart()` | Recreate the current code, reset clock | Replace with a new initial game of that deal |
| `loadBoard(code)` | Trim and parse code; reset clock only on success | Replace, or publish invalid-code notice |
| `loadSnapshot(text)` | Decode complete state; reset clock only on success | Import replacement, or publish invalid-snapshot notice |
| `exportSnapshot()` | Synchronize active clock | Encode latest game and return text |
| `activate(index)` | Synchronize active clock | Apply session activation |
| `resume()` | Reset observation baseline | Clear pause and load feedback |

The exposed load methods return a boolean. `BoardCodeForm` uses that result to move focus only after successful loading. Snapshot loading is a button action on the current textarea string, so it does not replace the draft with a normalized serialization automatically.

The private `notice(feedback)` helper changes both message fields and increments `announcement` while preserving the game. It does not bump generation or reset the clock. An invalid submission therefore leaves progress and board focus lifetime intact.

## Logical ticks

`tickSession(session, generation, milliseconds)` returns unchanged data when the captured generation differs from the current one or when the session is paused. It then delegates to `advanceGame`. If that function returns the existing game, the existing session is returned too.

A logical tick can update elapsed time and close a mismatch. It does not publish a new turn result, save a score or create a fresh board. Those decisions remain with activation and replacement. This small contract makes it possible to test stale-callback rejection without starting a browser timer.

The hook applies an additional generation check before obtaining an observation. Its effect has an active flag and clears scheduled work at cleanup. Session rejection is the final data-level protection, not the only lifecycle defense. [Clock design](clock-design.md) details scheduling, visibility and fractional steps.

## Preferences and effects

`Preferences` contains `size` and `bestMoves`. The key is `neon-pairs.preferences.v1`, and the stored object includes `schemaVersion: 1`. A valid size comes from `GRID_SIZES`; each best score uses a canonical size key and a finite safe integer count between that board's pair count and `MOVES_MAX`.

`rememberBest` returns the original preferences when an existing score is less than or equal to the new count. Otherwise it returns a new preferences object and best map. This reference stability means an ordinary clock tick or an equal result need not trigger another preference effect.

`useSavedPreferences` runs `writePreferences` after preference or store changes. Writing is intentionally outside the transition functions. A session activation can decide the new best without synchronously depending on browser storage. The writer catches failures, so the in-memory game remains playable even when persistence fails.

The reader returns a complete fallback on invalid saved content, including an invalid entry within the best map. It does not salvage a subset of scores from a partly invalid preference object. The writer touches only its own key, and the store interface has no removal or enumeration method.

## Focus is a neighboring concern

The board hook owns its remembered index; `Game` coordinates Resume through the board's limited focus ref before calling the controller. Replacement remounts the board through generation, while Resume retains it. Form drafts likewise remain local to controls. [React boundaries](react-boundaries.md) explains those lifetimes without adding presentation state to the session.

## Evidence and investigation

`session.test.ts` covers stale generations, paused activations and ticks, completion through play, completed imports and repeated feedback events. It checks that a final imported unfinished game can record a best, and it checks capped move counts. Its feedback snapshot test uses a JSON fixture.

`storage.test.ts` supplies stores that work and stores whose methods throw. Browser environment tests additionally make acquisition of localStorage fail. This separates the browser integration failure from validation and operation failures in the narrow store interface.

For an incorrect result, inspecting `activateCard` establishes the game transition first. If the game is right but the notice, celebration or preference is wrong, `activateSession` and `replaceGame` are the next places to inspect. If the data is right but an interaction sees old values, the controller's synchronization and commit path become relevant. The directory's separation makes those questions answerable without debugging the entire component tree at once.

# Acceptance
Acceptance is a set of journeys that checks whether Neon Pairs meets its product requirements.

Status: spec version 2.2.

Finish a game, then start another one during a mismatch. The first journey checks play and completion. The second checks that an earlier timer can't change a new game.

## Play

Use these journeys with the requirements in [Rules](../gameplay/rules.md):

- Finish every supported size with complete pairs.
- Reveal one card twice, then reveal a different card. Check the exact move count.
- Match a pair, then miss a pair. Check the immediate match and the 800ms active mismatch interval.
- Hide the page during a mismatch, then return and finish its remaining interval.
- Start and restart during a mismatch. Check the cleared state and later timer updates.
- Finish games with better, equal and worse move counts. Reload and check the current size's best.

## Controls

Use pointer, touch and keyboard to follow [Input](../interface/input.md) and [Controls](../interface/controls.md). Check control labels, row movement, edge stops, native Tab exit and focus after each action. Check that hidden cards reveal no identity in the DOM.

Follow the keyboard journey in I17 and check its accessibility tree. During user acceptance, confirm spoken results with a screen reader, including consecutive identical results and the final match with its win.

## Appearance

Measure the layout and review all 128 faces against [Visuals](../visuals/visuals.md). Use a 44px grayscale face sheet to distinguish shape, marker and fill. Check 16x16 boards at both stated viewport sizes, full focus outlines and the equivalent zoom layout. Check reduced motion and the static completion banner after its single pulse.

Play through completion and reset while checking [Sound](../sound/sound.md). Every action stays silent.

## Reproduction

Check [Reproducibility](../sharing/reproducibility.md) with its example deck and replay. Check snapshot round trips and malformed input. Check the exact mismatch timeout before an equal-time replay action.

Load an unfinished snapshot, attempt input while paused, then Resume. Check its remaining active time and focus. Load a completed snapshot and check its static banner and unchanged best score.

## Delivery

Use a locked install, type check, unit tests and a fresh browser build as defined in [Technology](../architecture/technology.md). Open the resulting HTML directly from disk with network access blocked. Use a local HTTP origin for saved preferences.

Review the pure game functions, browser effects, file sizes and behavior placement against [Architecture](../architecture/architecture.md).

Back to [Neon Pairs](../README.md).

# Test strategy
This page explains how Neon Pairs divides evidence between game tests, browser journeys, source checks and user acceptance.

The product contract is specification version 2.2. The README records a successful named compatibility run. [Known issues](known-issues.md) tracks verification limits, and [Fixtures](fixtures-guide.md) explains why replacing reviewed JSON expectations with current output would weaken the evidence.

## Start with the question

A deck test asks whether a code produces the published cards. A browser test asks whether a player can reach and activate those cards through rendered controls. An accessibility-tree capture asks what Chromium exposes to assistive software. None can substitute for the others.

The useful division follows the architecture's existing boundaries:

| Question | Existing evidence | What it cannot establish |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Does a turn change the right data? | Vitest tests beside `game.ts` | Native focus, scrolling or pointer dispatch |
| Does the seeded deal match the format? | Literal vectors and `tests/deal-oracle.ts` | Whether hidden identities leak into markup |
| Does the browser adapter count active time? | Pure clock tests plus controlled browser clocks | Real device scheduling latency |
| Can a player finish through the interface? | Built-page keyboard and touch journeys | Spoken screen-reader output |
| Does local storage survive reload? | HTTP-origin persistence journeys | Cross-browser behavior of disk-origin storage |
| Does the distribution stand alone? | Offline disk navigation and built-output inspection | Every browser engine or operating system |
| Does the layout survive difficult geometry? | Large-board, scrollbar, zoom and focus tests | Every possible window size |

This is a map of current checks, not a demand to create one test of each kind for every change. A correction to snapshot validation usually needs parser evidence first. A clipped focus ring needs browser geometry. A change to explanatory copy may need only the relevant reviewed expectation and a visual check. [Unit tests](unit-test-guide.md) and [Browser tests](browser-test-guide.md) show the local conventions.

## Pure behavior carries the broad matrix

`vitest.config.ts` includes `src/**/*.test.ts` and `scripts/**/*.test.ts`. The package's `test` script is `vitest run`. Most of these tests import `test` from Vitest and assertions from `node:assert/strict`. They do not mount React to prove a card transition.

The core state includes the immutable board description, its deck, matched positions, selection, moves, elapsed milliseconds and the started flag. Selection has closed, one-card and mismatch branches. Tests exercise transitions directly, allowing exact questions such as whether advancing a pending miss by 799ms leaves it open and whether the next millisecond closes both cards.

The suite checks complete pairs at all seven supported sizes. `completion.test.ts` finishes each size through `activateCard`; it does not infer that a 4x4 success proves a 16x16 finish. `deck.test.ts` checks the published seed-one vector, generator states, the inclusive maximum seed, frozen data and independent generation at each size. `deck-rejection.test.ts` targets uncommon rejection-sampling boundaries using separately stored expected decks.

The game tests also make negative cases visible. A fractional or out-of-range card index returns the old state. Repeating the first selected card adds no move. During a miss, every activation is ignored. Invalid elapsed steps leave the game unchanged. Keeping the original object in those cases is observable behavior in these tests; asserting identity can distinguish an ignored action from an unnecessary reconstruction.

Snapshot and replay tests carry a different matrix: exact object fields, integer ranges, byte limits, valid selections and action ordering. A round trip is useful, but two matching mistakes can round trip successfully. Independent expected fields and malformed inputs provide the stronger evidence. A valid started game with one revealed card and zero moves is the baseline for several invalid-counter cases, so rejection can be attributed to the changed counter rather than an unrelated invalid state.

## Session tests connect results to browser-independent policy

`src/game/session/session.ts` is a data adapter. Its tests create sessions and call `activateSession`, `replaceGame` and `tickSession` directly. This makes several integration rules cheap to check without pretending to test browser effects.

A replacement increments `generation`. A tick carrying an earlier generation has no effect. An unfinished imported game is paused and cannot accept card input or active time until resumed. A locally completed game can improve the appropriate saved move record. A completed import follows the import path instead of the live completion path. These are separate causes even when both render a completed board.

Session feedback tests inspect event progression as well as text. Two misses with the same wording still represent two turns. Focus movement and time advancement do not represent new turn results. Browser announcement tests then verify that these data changes become the intended DOM updates. Checking both layers helps distinguish a missing session event from a rendering problem.

Storage tests use the narrow `PreferenceStore` interface. A Map-backed implementation covers round trips and per-size minima; a throwing implementation covers failures without a browser. Browser tests separately exercise a denied `window.localStorage` getter. The distinction matters because failure while obtaining the store occurs before either `getItem` or `setItem` can run.

## Browser journeys use the shipped shape

The package's `test:e2e` command runs the main build, builds diagnostic entries, and then invokes Node's test runner over `tests/*.e2e.test.ts` with concurrency set to one. Playwright drives Chromium, while `node:test` owns the tests. There is no Playwright Test project configuration controlling this suite's retry or worker behavior.

Most journey files import the wrapper in `tests/browser-test.ts`. It launches a browser, creates a fresh context per case, collects page errors and closes resources. `tests/artifact-server.ts` serves the freshly built HTML on a private loopback port. `GAME_URL` points at the same build on disk. Persistence journeys use the served URL; offline-delivery checks use the disk URL.

Fresh contexts isolate browser storage, permissions and page-installed instrumentation. They do not make every global resource independent: the artifact server and browser belong to file-level hooks, and the runtime record has a shared output location. The serial command is part of the implementation being documented. [Flaky-test notes](flaky-test-notes.md) discuss the timing consequences.

The browser tests use public controls to load `np1-4-1`. They know its deck from the documented format and test fixture, rather than asking the application for hidden state. The board's hidden buttons expose positions and closed state. The tests inspect that absence directly in `input-contract.e2e.test.ts`, including the neutral back and lack of face artwork. A solver that depended on hidden SVGs would invalidate this evidence.

## Contract checks complement shared labels

Ordinary journey helpers import the control-label constants so they can focus on behavior. Contract tests also contain literal labels and limits. This prevents changing a production constant and every test lookup together from silently changing the public contract.

`control-contract.e2e.test.ts` covers native reproduction controls, their input limits, invalid statuses and action focus. `product-contract.e2e.test.ts` covers status presentation, continuing minutes and successful load size selection. `persistence-contract.e2e.test.ts` checks record comparisons, saved sizes and fresh progress after reload. These overlap broader journeys at specific seams, where a shared helper could otherwise conceal a mistake.

Overlap is useful when the assertions answer different questions. Loading a snapshot appears in parser tests, session tests and browser tests because validation, paused data and Resume focus are different behaviors. Repeating the same serializer implementation as an expected-value helper would add little protection. The suite's independent literal expectations are intended to break that circularity.

## Visual and accessibility evidence are concrete

The art entry renders every face at the minimum card size. Tests capture color, grayscale and neutral versions. Neutral silhouettes are compared for uniqueness, and separate assertions inspect marker geometry and palette application. This establishes machine-distinguishable geometry; a person still reviews whether the distinctions are usable. [Accessibility audit](accessibility-audit.md) explains that limit.

Layout tests inspect page width, card bounds, board scrolling and complete focus outlines. The large-board checks cover 360x800 and 1280x800 CSS-pixel viewports. A separate equivalent-zoom journey uses 640x400 with device scale 2. Visible-scrollbar cases remove Chromium's default scrollbar-hiding launch argument and test widths where scrollbar space changes the available board area.

The accessibility journey uses the Chromium DevTools Protocol to capture the accessibility tree during a complete keyboard game. It checks controls, revealed and matched names, disabled state exposure, results, completion, Tab exit and a fresh game. The artifact records browser and Playwright versions and explicitly records that a screen reader was not run. User acceptance owns the spoken journey. Tree assertions support that review; they do not prove speech delivery.

## Source and delivery checks

`source-audit.test.ts` inspects package pins, lockfile agreement, compiler settings and source conventions required by the architecture and technology specifications. It reads authored files rather than the compiled bundle. `source-conventions.test.ts` checks current export ownership, question-shaped predicate names, behavior-oriented test names and the small set of environment reads the runners use.

These are text checks with intentionally limited reach. The core effect scan names particular source files. It is not an analysis of every transitive call. The TypeScript source scan can reject spelling patterns, but cannot prove full semantic purity. Review remains necessary when moving behavior to a new module. [Code review](../architecture/code-review-guide.md) and [Source audit notes](../architecture/source-audit-notes.md) provide related architectural context.

The built-output test searches the emitted HTML for `fetch(` and the preload helper's `relList` marker. The offline journey blocks network access and checks that only the document request occurs while a card remains playable. Together they cover bundle content and observed loading. Neither measures first-render duration; [Performance budget](performance-budget.md) documents that evidence gap.

## Following through

Choose the smallest test that exposes the changed behavior, then follow it into the browser where native interaction or effects matter. [Regression catalogue](regression-catalogue.md) shows paired investigations, and [Release checklist](release-checklist.md) assembles the complete verification sequence. The remaining evidence gaps are tracked in [Known issues](known-issues.md).

# Unit test guide
This guide describes the small, direct tests used for Neon Pairs game data, parsers, session policy and developer commands.

The tests are ordinary TypeScript modules selected by Vitest. They use explicit inputs and inspect returned values. Most assertions come from `node:assert/strict`, while `test` comes from `vitest`. React and browser fixtures are reserved for behavior that needs a browser. The division is explained in [Test strategy](test-strategy.md).

## Discovery and execution

`vitest.config.ts` includes `src/**/*.test.ts` and `scripts/**/*.test.ts`. `npm test` runs `vitest run`. The browser files under `tests/` are outside that include set; their Node test runner is described in [Browser test guide](browser-test-guide.md). A file called `.e2e.test.ts` is not automatically a Vitest case in this project.

`npm run typecheck` is a separate check across app, Node and e2e compiler projects. Bundling is not the type checker. A successful unit run therefore does not establish that JSX, browser helpers or compiler project boundaries are correct. The release command sequence retains both checks.

Run the tests in a complete writable checkout with their reviewed JSON inputs. Running only fixture-independent cases may help diagnosis, but it cannot produce a complete suite result. [Fixtures guide](fixtures-guide.md) distinguishes inline data from reviewed files.

## A useful test exposes a decision

`game.test.ts` begins with `createGame(EXAMPLE_CODE)`, activates a card and checks the resulting selection, started flag and moves. It then tries invalid indices and repeat activation. This makes the decision boundary visible: a valid first reveal starts play, while ineligible input keeps the existing state.

A representative test can be read without opening React:

```ts
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
import { test } from 'vitest';
import { activateCard, createGame } from './game.ts';
import { EXAMPLE_CODE } from './game.fixture.ts';

test('a repeated first selection preserves the current state', () => {
  const first = activateCard(createGame(EXAMPLE_CODE), 2);
  assert.equal(activateCard(first, 2), first);
  assert.equal(first.moves, 0);
});
```

This example uses the existing style. Identity equality is meaningful here because `activateCard` explicitly returns its input for an ignored activation. Deep equality is appropriate when comparing reconstructed data such as a decoded snapshot. Replacing all identity assertions with structural comparisons would lose that distinction.

The current test titles describe behavior in plain language. Requirement references appear in some assertion messages, which helps trace a failure back to the specification without making the title depend on an ID. The source-convention check also inspects these names.

## Deterministic deck evidence

`game.fixture.ts` supplies the published code `np1-4-1`, its deck, known pairs, the first generator states and literal format constants. The deck is:

```text
6, 7, 0, 5, 2, 2, 0, 5, 3, 7, 1, 6, 4, 4, 1, 3
```

Indices 2 and 6 form a match. Indices 0 and 1 form a miss. Using these facts makes a transition test independent of deck inspection in the browser and easy to verify against the specification.

`deck.test.ts` checks generator states, complete pair counts, supported sizes, maximum seed and frozen board data. Its per-size loops do more than count cards: they also compare generation against `specDeal` from `tests/deal-oracle.ts`. That oracle uses BigInt arithmetic and is kept apart from production deck generation.

An independent algorithm and a literal example serve different purposes. The literal catches a shared misunderstanding of the algorithm; the wider oracle comparisons catch errors that the small example does not reach. The rejection-sampling tests add stored vectors for a draw above the accepted range and a draw exactly at the limit. Ordinary seeds may never exercise either branch during a short run.

The board-code parser tests are strict about grammar. A trailing line break, surrounding space, leading zeros, exponent notation and unsupported sizes are invalid at the core boundary. The Board code UI separately trims surrounding whitespace before calling the parser. A parser test that copied that UI trimming would blur two intentionally different responsibilities.

## State transitions and invariants

The core exposes `createGame`, `activateCard`, `advanceGame`, `isWon` and `faceUpCards`. Tests operate on immutable states and keep earlier states available for comparison. A new reveal should not mutate an earlier game's matched array or selection.

The turn tests cover the three selection branches directly. A match immediately adds two positions to `matched`, closes the selection and costs one move. A miss enters a mismatch with `remainingMs` equal to 800. All activations are ignored while that interval is pending. `advanceGame` handles the common active-time step for elapsed time and remaining mismatch time.

Boundary evidence is especially useful here. Advancing to just before closure, then to closure, distinguishes a real interval from an approximate timer. Invalid time inputs include nonfinite or nonpositive values. Time before the first reveal and time after completion have no effect. The pure tests can assert those facts exactly without scheduling a real timeout.

`completion.test.ts` finishes every supported size. It groups the deterministic deck into face pairs and activates both members of each pair. That use of generated data is appropriate because the question is whether all pairs complete the game, while separate deck tests establish the deal. It would be circular if used as the only proof of shuffle correctness.

## Counter caps remain playable states

`move-cap.test.ts` creates progress near or at the move limit. It checks reaching 999999, matching and completion at the cap, pending-miss closure and continued snapshot export. A cap test that checked only the displayed number could miss a state that refuses every later action.

`elapsed-time.test.ts` similarly checks the elapsed maximum of 359999999ms, import rejection above that maximum and continued play at the cap. The relevant behavior is bounded data with normal transitions, rather than a special end-of-game condition. Best-score storage tests also exercise the move cap, because a value accepted by live play needs consistent persistence handling.

These cases construct states directly for speed and precision. They do not require simulating hundreds of thousands of turns or waiting days. When the constructed state is also used as snapshot input, it still needs to satisfy the format's other invariants. A deliberately invalid fixture can otherwise cause a parser failure before the cap condition is reached.

## Validate one inconsistent fact at a time

`snapshot.test.ts` has a small `snapshot(overrides)` builder that starts with a complete version 1 object. It serializes the baseline and applies explicit overrides. This keeps malformed cases readable while preserving all unrelated fields.

The started-zero-move case needs care. A started game with no moves is valid only with one selected card. Testing a negative elapsed value on a started, closed, zero-move baseline would produce two reasons for rejection. The existing `ONE_REVEALED` baseline avoids that ambiguity and first asserts that the valid form is accepted.

Other cases cover whole matched pairs, duplicate indices, out-of-range selections, selecting a matched position, extra keys, pending misses with equal faces, and insufficient moves for progress. `snapshot-selection.test.ts` isolates selection and matched-position validation so a nested-field failure can be understood separately from outer-object validation.

Serialization tests check that exported fields match `SNAPSHOT_KEYS`, that matched positions are normalized without changing source order, and that fractional active time remains importable after export. A pending miss with a quarter millisecond remaining is serialized as a positive whole-millisecond interval, preserving a valid pending state. The exact browser-clock arithmetic is covered separately.

`saved-format.test.ts` checks UTF-8 byte measurement before parsing. ASCII padding can reach a byte boundary conveniently, while multibyte examples distinguish bytes from JavaScript string length. The snapshot limit is 65536 bytes; replay has its own larger limit. These are product format limits, not new test-only limits.

## Replay order and command behavior

`replay.test.ts` advances the logical timeline before each action. It checks a late first reveal, ignored activations and a mismatch deadline equal to the next action timestamp. `replay-order.test.ts` concentrates on equal-time array order, where reordering actions can change which card remains selected.

The replay state calculation is pure. The CLI tests in `scripts/replay.test.ts` cover a different seam: file arguments, working-directory resolution, stdout, stderr and exit status. They create temporary directories and files, invoke the command, and remove the test directories afterward. A command that computes the correct final state but prints an npm banner on stdout fails its machine-readable contract.

The relative-path test invokes the npm script from a caller folder and checks failure messages against a reviewed message fixture. Its distinction between unreadable files, malformed JSON and rule-invalid data is tested at the command boundary. None of this requires adding replay controls to the browser interface.

## Session and storage fakes are small

`session.test.ts` composes game calls with preferences and feedback. It checks stale generations, imported pause behavior, event progression and live completion. The tests can hold two sessions at once and prove that a callback meant for one cannot alter the other. The browser lifecycle suite then checks actual scheduled work and cleanup.

`storage.test.ts` provides a Map-backed `PreferenceStore` with only `getItem` and `setItem`. It covers separate minima for each size, equal and worse scores, malformed JSON, unsupported sizes and invalid score data. A throwing store verifies exception handling. A null store covers an unavailable adapter.

There is no need to fake the entire browser storage API for those unit cases. The missing getter-access failure is handled by a real browser init script in `browser-environment.e2e.test.ts`. Keeping each fake close to the behavior prevents an elaborate imitation from becoming another implementation to debug.

## Presentation logic without rendering

`card-state.test.ts` tests the text and state returned by `describeCard`. Hidden-card labels identify row, column and closed state. Revealed and matched labels add the known face and state. The file reads a reviewed expectation so changes to production face descriptions do not automatically rewrite the expected names.

`keyboard.test.ts` checks row and column boundaries and modifier handling through `navigationTarget`. The pure result can establish an intended destination, but cannot prove that native focus moves there or that scrolling preserves its outline. Those checks belong to the browser suite.

`face-design.test.ts` checks 128 unique identities through shape, marker and fill, table-derived parts and reviewed geometry. Browser screenshots add rendered evidence. A unit assertion about SVG coordinates and a neutral screenshot about rendered silhouette complement each other; neither is a full human distinguishability review.

## Source checks and follow-through

`source-audit.test.ts` and `source-conventions.test.ts` run in the same Vitest command but inspect source and package data rather than game states. [Test strategy](test-strategy.md) describes their coverage and text-scanning limits.

The strongest unit case usually starts with a small valid state, changes one relevant fact and expects a clearly different result. Browser evidence follows where the behavior crosses into native interaction or effects. [Regression catalogue](regression-catalogue.md) gives examples of those paired investigations.

# Browser test guide
This guide explains the Node and Playwright harness used to exercise Neon Pairs through its built browser interface.

The suite opens generated HTML, not the Vite development page. It uses Node's test runner and Playwright's browser automation library. That combination explains several otherwise surprising details: tests import a local `test` wrapper, the package command controls file concurrency, and browser assertions have a locally configured timeout. Start with [Test strategy](test-strategy.md) for the reason each layer exists.

## The normal entry point

From a writable project checkout, the complete command is:

```sh
npm run test:e2e
```

In `package.json`, this expands to:

```sh
npm run build && npm run build:art && node --test --test-concurrency=1 "tests/*.e2e.test.ts"
```

`build` performs type checking before Vite emits `dist/index.html`. `build:art` emits `.art/index.html` and `.session/index.html` through separate configurations. A failure in either build stops the command before the test runner. This prevents accidentally testing an older distribution after a failed compile.

The commands write build outputs and browser artifacts, so they need a writable checkout with the reviewed JSON expectation files consumed by the tests; see [Known issues](known-issues.md). The README records a successful run.

During focused development, invoking Node for one browser file can shorten diagnosis after a current build exists. Such an invocation does not perform the build chain by itself and does not replace the full release command. A failure that disappears only when old output is used remains a failure of the source being reviewed.

## What the wrapper owns

`tests/browser-test.ts` imports `before`, `after` and `test` from `node:test`. Its file-level setup creates `.browser-work` and `test-results`, sets `TEMP` and `TMP` for browser work, obtains version information and launches headless Chromium. It then starts the private artifact server.

The exported `test` accepts a name, an async body, optional browser-context options, a scrollbar mode and a timeout. The body receives `browser`, `context`, `page` and `gameURL`, plus an artifact helper. Each case gets a new context and page. The context is registered for cleanup with the Node test context. The wrapper also collects uncaught page errors and expects the collection to be empty after the body completes.

A failed assertion can end the body before that final page-error assertion, so the final check is not a universal crash report. Browser automation errors and page errors are different sources of failure. Looking at the first meaningful failure usually gives a better diagnosis than reading only the trailing timeout.

The `after` hook closes the normal browser, any lazily created visible-scrollbar browser, and the server. Tests creating an extra context themselves close it explicitly, as the phone completion journey does in a `finally` block. This is practical resource ownership, not an assumption that process exit will always clean up successfully.

## Disk and HTTP URLs answer different questions

`GAME_URL` in `tests/game-fixture.ts` is a file URL for `dist/index.html`. `ART_URL` and `SESSION_URL` similarly address diagnostic builds. Disk loading is the delivery path: the game should remain playable without sibling assets or network requests.

`gameURL`, supplied by the wrapper, is the HTTP origin from `serveArtifact`. The server reads the emitted HTML, listens on `127.0.0.1` using an available port, serves `/`, and returns 404 for other paths. It does not serve source, fixture JSON or a diagnostic API. Saved-preference tests use this stable origin within their context so reload can observe the same local storage.

A persistence test that uses the disk URL can become dependent on browser-specific storage treatment. A delivery test that uses only HTTP can miss a file-loading problem. Existing tests deliberately use both paths. [Browser support](browser-support.md) describes the resulting compatibility claims; [Storage testing](../persistence/storage-testing-guide.md) covers the persistence contract in more depth.

## Load a deterministic deal through the controls

`loadFixedBoard(page, url)` navigates, opens the native reproduction disclosure, fills Board code with `np1-4-1`, selects Load board, closes the disclosure and expects 16 cards. Its default URL is the built disk file. Tests that need HTTP pass the wrapper's `gameURL` explicitly.

The helper does not expose the application's state. Its pair positions come from `src/game/game.fixture.ts`, whose literal deck matches the published format example. This supports complete games while keeping hidden cards anonymous to the DOM. `play.e2e.test.ts` checks that closed cards have no SVG face and that diagnostic face attributes are absent before solving.

A compact behavior case follows the existing style:

```ts
import { expect, test } from './browser-test.ts';
import { loadFixedBoard, moves } from './game-fixture.ts';

test('a repeated first reveal leaves the move count at zero', async ({ page }) => {
  await loadFixedBoard(page);
  const card = page.locator('.card').nth(2);
  await card.click();
  await card.click();
  await expect(page.locator('.card.revealed')).toHaveCount(1);
  expect(await moves(page)).toBe(0);
});
```

The example uses the known deal, a native user action and observations available in the interface. The expected result does not call the implementation being tested.

## Selectors follow the observation

Control actions generally use accessible roles or labels with exact names. The size control is a combobox. Board code is a labeled input. Snapshot JSON is a labeled textarea. The disclosure uses a native summary element. These selectors exercise the same discoverability that a keyboard or assistive-software user needs.

`.card` and state classes are useful when inspecting card counts, position order and geometry. A positional locator is appropriate because the format defines row-order indices. It should not become a way to discover hidden identities. Card identity expectations come from the deterministic input, not an undocumented browser global.

Shared label constants keep ordinary journeys readable, but literal contract cases protect the actual wording. Changing a control's constant can otherwise change the test lookup and production label together. The dedicated contract files are deliberate independent evidence, rather than duplicate stylistic preferences.

## Time is a controlled input

`loadTimedBoard` installs Playwright's clock before navigation, loads the fixed deal and pauses at a later clock value. Time-sensitive journeys then use `page.clock.runFor` for exact active intervals. One test opens a miss, advances 200ms, hides the page, advances 2000ms while hidden, returns and checks the remaining 599ms plus 1ms boundary.

Headless Chromium keeps its tabs visible in this environment. The visibility tests therefore override `document.hidden` and dispatch `visibilitychange`, exercising the adapter input the game actually reads. Opening another tab is not a reliable substitute for this setup.

The fractional-clock file uses a narrower instrument: an init script replaces `performance.now` and a test-only event changes its reading. It can advance time and issue a click in the same browser task. That reproduces an overdue mismatch even if the scheduled callback has not run. The test proves synchronization before activation rather than measuring how quickly a timer fires on the host.

`exportedSnapshot` uses the visible export control and parses its textarea. Export synchronizes active time, so it can observe more than the most recent status render. This is useful for clock evidence, but it can also hide an idle-return bug if called during every wait. The idle-clock cases deliberately make no intermediate reads while hidden or paused. See [Flaky-test notes](flaky-test-notes.md) for the distinction.

## Focus needs a real journey

Calling `.focus()` is useful to establish a starting position. It does not prove that Tab can enter the board naturally. The keyboard and accessibility journeys include real Tab, Shift+Tab, arrow, Enter and Space events. Edge assertions check that arrows stop rather than wrap; Tab exit checks that the board does not trap focus.

The `moveKeyboardTo` helper reads only the currently focused card, computes row and column deltas and presses one arrow per step. It neither activates the destination nor reads its face. Matched cards remain reachable, and their disabled action state is checked separately from their focusability.

`focus-bounds.ts` measures card rectangles against the board viewport and window. It includes outline width and outline offset, along with viewport client borders, so a visible card with a clipped ring does not pass as fully visible. The quarter-pixel comparison allowance handles geometry rounding. It does not weaken card target-size assertions.

The pointer-focus cases deliberately click a sliver of a card near the board edge. They use mouse coordinates or touchscreen taps after arranging scroll position. A locator click that automatically scrolls the target fully into view would erase the condition under test. Wheel cases wait for changing scroll position and then a sequence of stable frames before clicking.

## Layout modes and diagnostic entries

Context options configure viewport, device scale and touch emulation. Visible-scrollbar mode removes Chromium's default `--hide-scrollbars` argument; its tests establish that scrollbars occupy space before inspecting the board. [Browser support](browser-support.md) lists the actual configurations.

The face sheet and unmount harness are separate builds, with their own disk URLs. They keep diagnostic controls out of the game distribution. [Fixtures guide](fixtures-guide.md) explains how those entries support artwork and lifecycle observations.

## Artifacts and runtime records

The wrapper turns a test name into an alphanumeric-and-hyphen directory under `test-results`. `artifacts.outputPath` accepts a basename and rejects a path containing directories. Existing cases write face-sheet PNGs and an accessibility journey JSON file through this helper.

The runtime record is `test-results/browser-runtime.json`. It contains Node, npm, Playwright and Chromium versions, plus whether named-combination enforcement was requested. `NEON_PAIRS_NAMED_COMBINATION=1` adds an exact comparison to the named tool set. `PLAYWRIGHT_CHROMIUM_EXECUTABLE` selects an alternate executable, but the recorded browser version still determines what was actually tested.

There is no automatic trace or screenshot-on-every-failure configuration in this wrapper. The presence of a screenshot from another case does not prove the failed case captured its final state. Artifact names and content are evidence created by their specific tests. [Accessibility audit](accessibility-audit.md) describes the normalized tree artifact and its limits.

For a release, use the complete build-and-run command and interpret failures with their environment and fixture availability. For a local diagnosis, preserve the failing action order and control only the browser input needed to reproduce it. Those two habits keep a fast test useful without turning an incomplete run into a compatibility claim.

# Fixtures guide
This guide explains the deterministic data, reviewed expectations and browser helpers used by Neon Pairs tests.

The project uses several things called fixtures, with different responsibilities. A TypeScript constant can identify a known deal. A reviewed JSON file can hold independent expected output. A browser helper can load a page and perform actions. A generated PNG or accessibility-tree record is an artifact from a run. Confusing these roles can turn a regression test into a comparison of current code with itself.

## The published deal is the common anchor

`src/game/game.fixture.ts` contains `EXAMPLE_CODE`, `EXAMPLE_DECK`, `EXAMPLE_PAIRS`, `RANDOM_STATES` and `SPEC_VECTOR`. These are test data, not a browser endpoint. The example code is `np1-4-1`; its literal deck is:

```text
[6, 7, 0, 5, 2, 2, 0, 5, 3, 7, 1, 6, 4, 4, 1, 3]
```

The pair list groups positions by face in a convenient completion order:

```text
[2, 6], [10, 14], [4, 5], [8, 15],
[12, 13], [3, 7], [0, 11], [1, 9]
```

Indices are zero-based row-order positions. A first reveal at 2 and second at 6 makes a match. Revealing 0 and 1 makes a miss. These facts let tests choose a transition without reading hidden DOM identity. They also make failures reviewable against the published reproducibility example.

`SPEC_VECTOR` holds literal sizes, format versions, byte/action bounds, mismatch duration and maximum seed. Tests compare production constants with those values. Importing the production constant as the expected value would not provide the same independent check if that constant were changed incorrectly.

`RANDOM_STATES` holds the published initial generator states for seed 1. `deck.test.ts` advances the production generator and compares against the list. The deck vector then checks the shuffle result, so generator correctness and deck ordering are both visible.

## Independent generation covers more than the example

`tests/deal-oracle.ts` implements `specDeal(size, seed)` with BigInt arithmetic. It starts from paired face IDs, advances the specified generator and uses rejection sampling before each descending shuffle swap. It does not call production `generateBoard`.

The deck tests first establish that the independent implementation reproduces the literal example. They then compare production output with the oracle at every supported size. This gives the broader algorithm checks a fixed reference point rather than trusting an independent implementation merely because it is in a test folder.

Rare rejection branches use stored vectors in a separate JSON input. One covers a draw above the limit, and the other covers a draw exactly on it. Those cases exist because ordinary seed-one generation can pass even when a boundary comparison is wrong.

## Reviewed JSON inputs and their consumers

The following paths are all relative to the project root. They are source expectations, not files generated by the documented browser command.

| Expected file | Reader | What the reader compares or validates |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `scripts/package.fixture.json` | `scripts/source-audit.test.ts` | Installed package version expectations |
| `scripts/replay-messages.fixture.json` | `scripts/replay.test.ts` | stderr text for missing, malformed and rule-invalid replay files |
| `src/game/deck-rejection.fixture.json` | `src/game/deck-rejection.test.ts` | Independent complete decks for rejection boundaries |
| `src/game/board/card-state.fixture.json` | `src/game/board/card-state.test.ts` | Three hidden/revealed/matched descriptions |
| `src/game/board/face-design.fixture.json` | `src/game/board/face-design.test.ts` | Designs for face IDs 0, 64 and 9 |
| `src/game/session/session.feedback.fixture.json` | `src/game/session/session.test.ts` | Initial, mismatch, match and win feedback |
| `tests/ui.fixture.json` | `tests/ui-snapshot.ts` | Empty-best, banner, mismatch and winning-result text |
| `tests/accessibility.fixture.json` | `tests/accessibility-fixture.ts` | Complete journey names, results, controls and README record |
| `tests/status-format.fixture.json` | `tests/product-contract.e2e.test.ts` | Initial, matched and imported-completion status text |

The complete suite reads all nine reviewed files. Missing inputs prevent the affected tests from running. [Known issues](known-issues.md) records the impact.

Several readers parse JSON as `unknown` and narrow it. `accessibilityFixture` checks the numeric size, control strings, arrays of strings and several final fields before returning a typed object. `uiSnapshot` checks its four strings. Other tests compare parsed expectations directly with the actual structured value.

The card-state expectation covers hidden position 0, revealed position 6 with face 0 and matched position 15 with face 64. The face-design expectation samples the first solid face, its outlined counterpart and a diagonal-marker face. The all-face table test supplies broader coverage independently of those samples.

## A missing expectation is not an update request

If a test cannot read its JSON input, inspect the path and checkout contents before changing application code. Most paths use `new URL(..., import.meta.url)`, so they resolve beside the reader rather than from the shell's current folder. Changing the working directory will not recover a file absent from that module's directory.

Generating expected JSON from the current production function would make the suite runnable while discarding the review boundary. For example, a bad face label copied from `faceDesign` into its own expectation would pass. Recovering the reviewed input, or independently reviewing any intentional replacement against the specification, preserves the test's purpose.

The project does not expose an automatic “approve all snapshots” command in `package.json`. Its snapshot terminology includes explicit JSON expectations and the product's progress format, not only a testing framework feature. A snapshot test failure can therefore mean several different things; the reader and compared fields identify which one.

## State builders keep invalid cases precise

`snapshot.test.ts` has a local builder that serializes a complete valid initial progress object plus overrides. Later baselines represent started progress with one revealed card or a pending miss. The tests first accept those baselines and then change a counter or selection fact.

That approach avoids invalid-by-default fixtures. A started game with zero moves and a closed selection is already inconsistent. Adding a negative counter to it would not isolate the counter validation. The one-card baseline makes the intended reason for rejection visible.

Completed progress can be constructed from the literal pair positions. Larger completed states use every index, a closed selection, a sufficient move count and a started flag. Browser tests load those through Snapshot JSON when the question concerns presentation of imported completion, rather than spending time playing every large-board pair.

This is different from proving live completion. `completion.test.ts` and the browser play journey activate cards through the relevant action path. An imported completed board cannot establish that the final live turn records feedback, updates preferences or selects celebration correctly.

## Browser helpers act through public controls

`tests/game-fixture.ts` exports disk URLs for the game and both diagnostic entries. It also exports `PHONE`, the 360x800 viewport used by several journeys. The URL constants identify built outputs; the helper does not serve source itself.

`loadFixedBoard` navigates, opens Reproduce a game, fills the known code, loads it, closes the disclosure and checks the card count. Its optional URL argument lets a persistence case use the wrapper's HTTP origin instead of the default disk URL.

`loadTimedBoard` installs the Playwright clock before navigation, loads the same deal and pauses at a controlled later value. The later baseline keeps initialization separate from active play. Individual tests then advance time explicitly and choose when a valid reveal begins counting.

`moves` reads the displayed move value using its status label. `finishBoard` clicks the literal pair positions and checks the matched-card count. `exportedSnapshot` opens the disclosure, uses Export snapshot, parses the textarea, closes the disclosure and checks that the parsed value is an object.

Export is a public action, but it synchronizes active time before returning data. A test that repeatedly exports during an idle hidden interval may alter the observation pattern it is trying to investigate. The idle-clock cases therefore avoid those intermediate observations. [Flaky-test notes](flaky-test-notes.md) explains why that detail matters.

## Diagnostic builds are controlled observation points

The art and session Vite configurations emit separate HTML entries. The sheet captures all faces and compares card styles with the game; the session entry supplies Unmount game for timeout and subscription tracking. Their controls stay outside the distribution. [Browser test guide](browser-test-guide.md) explains loading and instrumenting them.

## Generated artifacts are results, not expectations

The wrapper creates a directory derived from each test's name under `test-results`. `outputPath` accepts a basename. Existing cases write `face-sheet-color.png`, `face-sheet-grayscale.png`, `face-sheet-neutral.png` and the accessibility journey record.

The tree record normalizes browser nodes and excludes environment-specific URLs and internal identifiers. It captures what the current browser exposed during that run, along with tool versions and the explicit absence of a screen-reader run. It is not loaded as the journey's reviewed expected output.

`browser-runtime.json` is another generated result, written by setup rather than by a particular visual case. It identifies the launched tools. A copied runtime record or old screenshot cannot establish that a new candidate passed. The documented command builds from current source to keep that connection understandable.

Keep these distinctions when diagnosing failures: literal vectors establish independent facts, local builders arrange states, helpers drive the interface, reviewed JSON holds expectations, and artifacts describe observations. [Unit test guide](unit-test-guide.md) and [Browser test guide](browser-test-guide.md) show how those parts fit into executable cases.

# Import safety policy
This page explains how Neon Pairs validates untrusted exchange text before a browser session or replay result can use it.

The important boundary is between a draft and accepted game data. A text field can contain arbitrary edits, and a replay file can contain arbitrary bytes decoded as text. Neither is treated as a `GameState` just because JSON parsing succeeds. Shape checks, numeric checks and game-specific consistency checks happen before the browser commits a replacement.

## Field diagnostics and the current implementation

A field outside a format's declared shape is a validation failure, including inside a selection or replay action. The diagnostic policy makes that particular mistake identifiable to a person correcting copied data. An import with a field its format doesn't define shows "Unknown field: NAME." for the first such field and leaves the current state unchanged. This applies to the field diagnostic; it does not make an incomplete object or an unsupported version acceptable. The format's own required fields and state constraints still determine acceptance.

The implementation already rejects extra keys, but does not yet produce that field-specific notice. `hasExactKeys` returns a boolean, `decodeSnapshot` returns `null`, and the browser displays `Invalid snapshot.` for all snapshot failures. `readReplay` provides problem categories rather than the offending key name. The current adapters reject extensions without identifying the offending field as the diagnostic policy requires.

The existing code does not define a traversal order, object-path syntax or combined-error format for a field-specific diagnostic. Its boolean exact-key helper cannot report a first key. Those details cannot be inferred from a `null` result. For current behavior, examine the published notice and replay problem category rather than expecting a key name.

## Validation before replacement

`useGame.loadSnapshot(text)` calls `decodeSnapshot(text)` first. A failed result calls the notice helper and returns `false`. Only a successful result reaches `clock.reset()` and `replaceGame(current.current, game, true)`. There is no earlier step that installs the imported code or clears the existing matched positions.

`useGame.loadBoard(code)` follows the same broad shape with a board-code parser. It trims the control's draft, checks the result, and only then resets the clock and constructs a replacement game. A valid board-code string is sufficient for a fresh deal; a snapshot needs the additional position checks because it claims progress.

Failure changes visible feedback and the announcement counter. It does not replace the game, reset the running clock, save a different size or discard the edited draft. “Keeps the game” therefore does not mean that every field of the containing `Session` has reference equality: notices are session fields too. Nor does it freeze the active game while someone corrects text. A running game can continue to gain elapsed time after an unsuccessful load.

This distinction is visible in `tests/control-contract.e2e.test.ts`: the test enters bad board and snapshot drafts, verifies the notices and retained text, then advances the clock and verifies that the prior game is still running. A test that expected elapsed time to remain fixed indefinitely after rejection would assert behavior the product does not have.

## The shared JSON boundary

The small helpers in `src/game/saved-format.ts` separate JSON mechanics from game validation:

| Helper | Meaning at this boundary |
| --- | --- |
| `isWithinBytes(text, maxBytes)` | Measures UTF-8 encoded length, inclusively |
| `parseJson(text)` | Returns parsed unknown data, or `undefined` after a parse exception |
| `isJsonObject(value)` | Accepts non-null objects except arrays |
| `hasExactKeys(value, keys)` | Checks own-key count and presence of every expected own key |
| `isNonnegativeSafeInteger(value)` | Accepts numeric safe integers greater than or equal to zero |

`JSON.parse` can produce `null`, a list, a string, a boolean or a number. Those are valid JSON texts and invalid snapshot or replay roots. The object guard is what distinguishes them from a malformed text error. This is especially visible in replay results: `{` produces `malformedJson`, whereas `null` produces `format`.

`parseJson` does not execute input as code. A string containing script-like characters is still a string and fails where an object or number is required. The decoder does not merge the parsed object into the live session wholesale. It constructs the accepted state from a generated board and the fields it has validated.

Exact keys are checked as a set, not as an ordering constraint. Missing fields fail as well as extra fields. Nested objects are checked at their own format boundaries. A `closed` selection with an `index` is invalid even if that index would be an eligible position in a different selection variant. A replay action with an annotation field is invalid even if `atMs` and `index` are otherwise good.

The helpers operate on the parsed object, not the original token stream. JSON duplicate property names are consequently handled by `JSON.parse` before exact-key checking; the decoder does not retain a record of earlier overwritten occurrences. Likewise, numeric notation such as `1.0` becomes the number `1`. The integer predicate checks the value it receives rather than enforcing a preferred spelling of a JSON number.

## Resource bounds are checked at the text boundary

Snapshot decoding measures its input before parsing and rejects text above `SNAPSHOT_MAX_BYTES`, which is `65_536`. Replay reading checks `REPLAY_MAX_BYTES`, which is `1_048_576`, before parsing. The replay parser then rejects more than `REPLAY_MAX_ACTIONS`, which is `10_000`. Trailing JSON whitespace is legal within the byte budget and still consumes that budget.

These checks bound the accepted format, but they should not be described as a streaming parser. `TextEncoder` allocates an encoded representation for measurement. The CLI also calls `readFile` before `readReplay` checks text size. A very large input can therefore already have been read into memory when it is rejected. The code provides explicit acceptance limits rather than a promise that arbitrary input has no allocation cost.

The browser textarea's `maxLength` is a separate character limit. Multibyte text can satisfy that limit and exceed the decoder's byte limit. The existing byte helper test uses an accented character to establish that bytes, rather than JavaScript string length, control acceptance. [Snapshot format](snapshot-format.md) discusses how this interacts with readable export text.

## Snapshot checks depend on the regenerated deal

After validating the version and board code, `decodeSnapshot` generates the board used to interpret positions. `readMatched` checks unique in-range positions and requires both copies of every represented face. An even-length list alone is not enough: on `np1-4-1`, `[2, 6]` is a pair while `[0, 1]` is not.

`readSelection` checks availability against that matched list. A mismatch needs different positions with different faces and an integer remaining interval from `1` through `800`. It cannot describe a same-face pair awaiting closure, because normal play resolves matching cards immediately. When every position is matched, availability also prevents any nonclosed selection.

The full decoder checks counter bounds, a minimum move count and consistency with `started`. These checks establish the stated constraints without reconstructing every earlier action. [Snapshot format](snapshot-format.md) gives the complete validation sequence; [Snapshot selection notes](snapshot-selection-notes.md) explains the board-dependent helpers.

## Replay checks and isolated evaluation

`readReplay` checks root shape, version, board code, action count and `endMs` before walking actions. Each action then needs its exact object shape, safe nonnegative numbers, a nondecreasing timestamp no later than `endMs`, and a position inside the deck. Its index into the action array is included in action-specific failures.

Evaluation can already have computed earlier actions when a later action fails. That is safe because the evolving state is local to `readReplay`; no browser session has been committed. The function returns a problem rather than that partial state. This is different from a streaming UI that visibly applies each imported action as it reads.

An in-range activation during a mismatch is valid replay data even though the game ignores it. So are an activation of an already matched card and a repeated activation of the current first card. Validation checks whether the action is well formed; `activateCard` decides whether it changes play. Treating every ignored activation as a corrupt replay would conflate these two jobs.

Action timestamps may be much larger than the elapsed clock cap. The replay evaluator advances the logical timeline using safe integers, while `advanceGame` caps the resulting elapsed counter. That distinction prevents a legitimate long timeline from being rejected merely because the visible clock has saturated. [Replay format](replay-format.md) explains exact timeout edges and equal-time order.

## Failure reports that preserve the evidence

For current snapshot failures the decoder deliberately supplies no reason. The most effective local investigation isolates a single change against a known accepted object: replace just the selection, just the code, or just one counter. The tests in `snapshot.test.ts` use this pattern so that an unrelated invalid baseline cannot hide a missing check.

Replay reports have more detail. `readReplay` distinguishes file size, JSON syntax, root format, board code, actions array, end time, individual action shape, time order and index bounds. The CLI translates these into stderr text and uses a one-based action number for readers. Internal action positions remain zero-based. Mixing these conventions can lead an engineer to inspect the wrong action.

Retaining original text matters when a failure depends on bytes or syntax. Parsing and reserializing a padded document can remove the very length excess that caused its rejection. A screenshot of a notice cannot establish whether an extra property was nested or at the root. For the current accepted shapes, use [Board code format](board-code-format.md), [Snapshot format](snapshot-format.md) and [Replay format](replay-format.md); for the browser steps around them, use [Sharing FAQ](sharing-faq.md).

docs/competition/competition-rounds.md:28:Consider the early part of an eight-person example. The group can still be in its first round while several people have already finished individual attempts. A mockup that advances a round label whenever the completion banner appears would conflate an individual game result with event progress. The existing completion banner reports a board finish; it contains no event interpretation.
docs/competition/competition-ties.md:78:`src/game/move-cap.test.ts` covers completion at the move boundary. The browser and core clock tests cover elapsed behavior separately. Those tests are evidence about single-game values; there is no competition result comparator test in the current source.
docs/competition/competition-research.md:18:The working setup was deliberately modest: one browser game, people seated close enough to see the screen and paper notes beside the device. Event sketches were discussed on paper because the game has no participant entry or bracket controller. The browser supplied the actual card play, its ordinary status area and the existing reproduction tools.
docs/competition/competition-research.md:72:This is relevant to the feel of local competition. The current application has no way to know who watched the screen or who spoke during a turn. No screen arrangement can make that social history part of the board code. The notes identify a design tension.
docs/competition/competition-deals.md:28:`boardCode(size, seed)` constructs a string and validates it through `parseBoardCode`, throwing for invalid input. `generateBoard(code)` parses the code, constructs a deck with each face twice and shuffles it. The returned board object and deck array are frozen. There is no participant input in this process.
docs/competition/competition-deals.md:48:`newGame` passes the current game's seed to that function. It prevents the immediate replacement from reusing the previous seed, but it supplies no collection of earlier codes. A sequence can therefore revisit an older seed after an intervening game. The helper has no event memory and no match context.
docs/competition/competition-pairing.md:13:Pairing connects a group of people to an event structure. It is separate from choosing a board, recording a finished attempt or interpreting a tied result. The game has no participant collection; competition extends the existing solo controller.
docs/competition/competition-scores.md:41:There are no participant names or board codes in that value. A best belongs to a board size across ordinary games, rather than to a particular generated deal. A person who sees the size-4 best is not seeing the result of the current board code unless the circumstances happen to coincide.
docs/competition/competition-scores.md:55:There is no competition argument or mode check in either function. The source therefore does not currently implement the boundary described on this page. This is a concrete integration gap, not an indication that `rememberBest` has the wrong behavior for its existing caller.
docs/competition/competition-overview.md:18:The game implements solo play. There is no competition entry form, bracket view, participant model or tournament controller in `src/game/Game.tsx`. That component composes the ordinary controls, status, board and reproduction panel around `useGame()`. Competition is a product extension that has not yet shipped.
docs/competition/competition-overview.md:20:This distinction matters during review. A prototype can show a convincing bracket around the existing board while still delegating all game actions to the ordinary session. That demonstrates a possible composition, but it says little about whether participant progress, handoffs and completion belong to the same coherent experience. The detailed pages identify the relevant behavior and the places where the current source offers support or creates a complication.
docs/competition/competition-overview.md:50:The core already separates game data from presentation. `src/game/game.ts` contains card transitions and logical elapsed time. `src/game/deck.ts` contains board parsing and deterministic generation. Those files have no participant knowledge. That makes them a useful basis for discussing competition without embedding group administration into card rendering.

open-forge:
  description: Game options and reproduction controls
  tags:
    - Game
    - Controls
---
# Controls
Controls is a specification that defines the game options and reproduction tools in Neon Pairs.

Status: spec version 2.2.

You can start another deal, repeat the current one or load saved progress. Each control keeps the same label, so you can find the same action after a game changes.

## Deal controls

The main controls are:

- C01 - Label the native size select "Grid size". Give it options `4x4`, `6x6`, `8x8`, `10x10`, `12x12`, `14x14` and `16x16`, with numeric side length `N` as each value. After a successful board-code or snapshot load, select the loaded board's size.
- C02 - Label the fresh-deal button "New Game". It creates a fresh seed and keeps the current size.
- C03 - Label the repeat-deal button "Restart". It starts the same board code again.

Changing size, starting and restarting follow the session rules in [Rules](../gameplay/rules.md).

## Reproduction tools

- C04 - Put reproduction controls inside a native `details` element that starts collapsed. Give its summary the exact text "Reproduce a game".

The controls use the board-code and snapshot formats defined in [Reproducibility](../sharing/reproducibility.md). A board code starts a deal. A snapshot loads progress on a deal.

## Load a board

- C05 - Label the text input "Board code" and limit it to 32 characters. Show the current board code after a new deal, Restart or a successful load. Keep an edited draft when a card action changes the game.

- C06 - Label its button "Load board". Validate the entered code before replacing the current game with that deal's starting state.

For example, loading `np1-4-1` starts its hidden four-column board. Entering that code alone keeps the current game until you select Load board.

## Snapshot tools

- C07 - Label the textarea "Snapshot JSON" and limit it to 65536 characters. The parser also applies the UTF-8 byte limit in the snapshot format.

- C08 - Label the export button "Export snapshot". Fill the textarea with readable version 1 snapshot JSON that you can select and copy manually. Export leaves the game state and clock unchanged. It requires no Clipboard API.

Export `elapsedMs` and a pending mismatch's `remainingMs` as whole milliseconds. A pending mismatch always exports at least 1ms.

- C09 - Label the import button "Load snapshot". Validate the complete draft before replacing the current game. Load unfinished progress paused and show "Loaded snapshot. Select Resume to continue." Load completed progress as completed without pausing and show "Loaded completed snapshot."

- C10 - Show a "Resume" button only while an imported unfinished game is paused. Selecting it clears that pause. Unfinished play continues from the loaded state. While paused, block every card activation and allow board focus movement. On Resume, move focus to the board's remembered tab stop before removing the Resume button. A loaded completed game stays completed and shows no Resume button.

- C11 - On invalid input, keep the current game and the entered draft for correction. Show the exact status for that control:

| Control | Status |
| --- | --- |
| Load board | Invalid board code. |
| Load snapshot | Invalid snapshot. |

- C12 - A loaded completed snapshot keeps the win banner static and plays no celebration. Import doesn't write a best score. Resuming an unfinished snapshot and later winning records a local best under R10.

For example, loading a completed game with fewer moves than the saved best shows that game without replacing the saved record.

## Focus

- C13 - Keep focus on the button used for starting, restarting, loading or exporting. These actions don't move focus to the board. Resume follows C10 because its button disappears. The board's remembered tab stop follows the focus rules in [Input](input.md#focus).

## Replay

- C14 - Keep replay in the developer CLI and game core. V1 has no replay controls in the game UI.

Run `npm run --silent replay -- PATH` to read a replay file. On valid input, print only the final snapshot JSON to stdout and exit 0. On invalid input, print nothing to stdout, write a message to stderr and exit nonzero.

The complete game pack starts in [Neon Pairs](../README.md).
