# Tables policy

This page records the markup policy for ordered result data and explains why the current game statistics use a different structure.

There is no result table in the current UI. `GameStatus.tsx` displays four properties of a single game in a definition list. Reproduction controls use forms, and the board is a CSS grid of buttons. None of those structures is evidence that ordered records have already been implemented.

## Policy for result data

When the content represents records with comparable columns, its relationships need to survive reading beyond the visual arrangement. CSS alone can align text while leaving those relationships absent from the document structure. Ranked or bracket data is a table element with a caption and th scope="col" header cells. The caption identifies the collection being read, while the column headers connect each record's values to their meaning.

This is a content-specific policy. It does not make the game board a data table because it has rows and columns, and it does not require converting every compact summary to tabular markup. The distinction begins with what the content means: interactive card coordinates, a property's value and a record in an ordered result collection are different things.

No such result feature is present in `Game.tsx`. The policy applies when result data is introduced. [Native controls guide](native-controls-guide.md) discusses the broader preference for native semantics without adding another result format.

## Why the statistics are a definition list

GameStatus renders Moves, Pairs, Time and Best as four `dt`/`dd` groups inside a `dl`. Each term names a property of the same current game. There are no peer result rows and no column whose meaning changes with the row being read.

The layout happens to use flex and can wrap. At a wide width, those groups may look like cells in a horizontal strip. At a narrow width, they can flow to multiple lines. Neither visual arrangement changes the definition-list relationship. Replacing the wrapper with a table solely to preserve one desktop arrangement would confuse layout with content structure.

The Best value is one saved move count selected by current size. It does not present a list of people or a comparison across many records. `session.preferences.bestMoves[String(game.size)]` chooses the value before it reaches GameStatus. A single local best is not an implemented ordered-results screen.

[Status bar](status-bar.md) documents those expressions and labels. The present statistics model has no result columns.

## Why the card board is not a table

Board renders a named region containing an inner `div.board` and native card buttons. CSS Grid places those buttons in row order. Each card has its own coordinate and state in its accessible name, and keyboard movement follows a dedicated spatial model.

The table policy does not turn that interactive surface into a data table. A card is activated, can reveal a face and participates in remembered focus. A result cell is read as part of a record. They have different purposes even if both appear in a rectangle.

There is also no ARIA grid role on the current board. Its native buttons and movement handler implement the specified interaction without declaring a separate composite widget role. [Board keyboard navigation](board-keyboard-navigation.md) traces that behavior. A review of result markup should not accidentally rename or restructure the card controls because the word “row” appears in both contexts.

## What the caption contributes

An ordered collection needs context. A visible title elsewhere on a page can be helpful, but a table caption directly identifies the collection associated with the table. That matters when reading the table independently or navigating between document structures.

The policy does not specify caption text. The source has no existing results title. A feature's actual subject supplies the wording. Describing that subject is different from attaching a technical explanation of table markup to product copy.

A caption also does not supply missing column meaning. A reader needs to know whether a number represents moves, a position in an ordering or another property. The required header cells carry the column relationships; the caption names the whole collection. Combining all labels into a caption would leave the row values harder to interpret.

## Column relationships and reading order

The `scope="col"` attribute makes the header's direction explicit. It communicates that the header applies to values down its column. A bold `td`, a styled `div` or text positioned above a column can look similar while having a different structure.

A reviewer can inspect the table DOM and the browser's accessibility representation separately from the screenshot. The screenshot establishes visible arrangement. The DOM establishes element choices and attributes. The accessibility view helps establish that the browser exposes a meaningful table structure. No single one of these views proves all aspects of the interface.

Row headers, column order, numeric alignment and sorting controls depend on the result feature. The current game has no result implementation with those details.

## Narrow layouts and long values

The current game already separates outer page width from board overflow. Result data would have its own content and width behavior; it cannot simply inherit the card board's scroll logic by sharing a class name. A table's relationship between headers and values remains meaningful even when its viewport is narrow.

There is no table stylesheet in the source and no prescribed responsive table transformation here. A reviewer can still observe whether a proposed layout makes values readable and associated with their headers. Changing a collection into a stack of unrelated labels solely at a breakpoint can affect more than appearance, so both DOM and visual behavior are relevant evidence.

Name text can also vary in width without changing its accepted value. Typography and wrapping are layout concerns. The name policies remain separate from table structure; accepted names retain their displayed representation. [Typography](../visuals/typography.md) and [Form layout guide](form-layout-guide.md) explain nearby layout decisions in the existing interface.

The existing accessibility journey covers game controls and completion, not a result table. Evidence for a future result view would identify its actual markup and readable rows; the current statistics tests cannot establish that structure. [Accessibility audit](../quality/accessibility-audit.md) provides the wider review context.

# Announcements policy

This page describes how event feedback is published, repeated and kept separate from routine game rendering.

The game has many visible updates, but only some represent a new result. A clock tick is a changing value; resolving a turn is an event. Treating those as the same kind of update would make a memory game noisy and would bury the information a player needs after selecting two cards.

## Publication point

`Game.tsx` places the game result between the board instructions and the Board itself. Its paragraph has `role="status"`, `aria-live="polite"` and `aria-atomic="true"`, with the current feedback inside a span. The page has exactly one live region, the status paragraph in Game.tsx. New status text, such as whose turn it is, goes through that region. The current game publishes pair results and load outcomes there; it has no turn-owner feature.

The paragraph remains mounted while its content changes. It is inside `.game-result`, which has a minimum height of `56px`, flex alignment and margins. The wrapper reserves a readable area near the board without making the scrollable card content itself the announcement source.

Polite publication allows the browser and assistive technology to schedule the result around other speech. Atomic content indicates that the paragraph's result is treated as a complete update rather than an isolated changed number. These attributes express the intended exposure; the actual spoken experience still needs user acceptance with a screen reader.

## Session data behind the paragraph

The session owns `feedback` and an integer `announcement`. Game renders `<span key={session.announcement}>{session.feedback}</span>`. Updating the key replaces the child span even when its text is identical to the preceding result. This gives repeated events a DOM change without adding a hidden counter to the spoken text.

The counter is event identity, not a statistic presented to the player. It does not track moves, matched pairs or elapsed seconds. A failed load can advance it without adding a move, while the first card reveal changes game state without advancing it.

A broad render counter would be wrong for this job. Session renders occur for time and selection changes that should not repeat the last turn result. The explicit event field makes the distinction inspectable in `session.ts` and `use-game.ts`.

## Turn results

`activateSession` calls the pure `activateCard`. If the game object is unchanged, it returns the current session. If the result has selection kind `one`, it returns the updated game without changing feedback or announcement identity. That covers the first eligible reveal.

After the second eligible reveal, the result is either a mismatch or a match. The session builds the appropriate text and increments `announcement`. Completion is checked at this same boundary, so the winning match gets a combined result rather than two competing event publications.

| Result | Text produced by the session |
| --- | --- |
| First matched pair | `Pair found. 1 pair matched.` |
| Later nonfinal pair | `Pair found. M pairs matched.` |
| Mismatch | `No match. Cards close after a short pause.` |
| Winning pair | `Pair found. All pairs found in N moves and time.` |

Here `M` and `N` are replaced with the actual counts, and `time` is the output of `formatElapsed`. The singular branch is based on `game.matched.length === 2`. The final branch takes precedence over the nonfinal pair count.

A card's accessible name also changes when it reveals or matches. That is the focused control describing its own state, not a second turn-result producer. The text in the event paragraph summarizes what the two-card attempt achieved. [Screen reader notes](screen-reader-notes.md) follows those two sources in a complete game.

## Consecutive identical results

Two misses in a row produce the same sentence. Updating only a string state can leave the DOM text unchanged, which gives no new mutation for the second event. The keyed span avoids relying on a different visible sentence to distinguish them.

The current sequence is concrete. Initial feedback is empty. Revealing index 0 on `np1-4-1` changes selection to `one` without publishing. Revealing index 1 produces a mismatch and advances the event identity. After the interval closes, choosing those two indices again produces the same text with a later identity.

The counter advances once for each resolved attempt in that sequence, not once for each card action or timer update. A third activation during the mismatch is ignored by the game and leaves the event unchanged. The same is true of a repeated activation on the first revealed card.

There is no temporary blanking timeout between identical results. The implementation does not clear text, wait a guessed number of milliseconds and restore it. That avoids adding announcement timing to the game clock or introducing a second lifecycle that can outlive a replacement game.

## Changes that stay quiet

`tickSession` advances the game and returns a new session with that game, leaving feedback and announcement fields intact. Mismatch closure is part of this advancement. It does not publish a new “cards closed” result. The earlier mismatch sentence already told the player that closure would follow a short pause.

Arrow movement is local board focus state. It does not call the session feedback path. Clock renders update Time in GameStatus, while card memoization prevents unchanged cards from rendering again. Neither operation is a new turn result.

New Game and Restart call `replaceGame` with `imported: false`. That replacement clears the prior feedback and load notice while keeping the announcement number. A successful board-code load follows the same replacement path. These operations clear old context; the current source does not add a success sentence for a board-code load.

Clearing text is still a DOM change and may appear in a mutation trace as an empty result. It is different from republishing a turn sentence. The accessibility journey's expected record includes the new-game clearing event, so a raw count of every mutation is not a substitute for reading what each event contains.

## Load outcomes share the publication path

The controller's `notice(feedback)` helper assigns both `feedback` and `loadNotice`, then increments `announcement`. Invalid Board code publishes `Invalid board code.`; invalid Snapshot JSON publishes `Invalid snapshot.`. Repeating the same invalid submission is a new load attempt and advances the identity again.

For valid snapshot import, `replaceGame(..., true)` increments the identity and publishes either `Loaded snapshot. Select Resume to continue.` or `Loaded completed snapshot.`. The former corresponds to a paused unfinished game, the latter to completed progress. Valid board-code loading does not use the imported-snapshot branch.

Reproduction also renders `loadNotice` in its ordinary paragraph with id `load-notice`. The load buttons reference it through `aria-describedby`. That keeps the outcome visible beside the text tools and associates the description with their actions without creating another event publisher in that panel.

Resume clears feedback and loadNotice without increasing the event identity. It also transfers focus to the board before its button disappears. [Reproduction panel](reproduction-panel.md) and [Focus policy](focus-policy.md) describe those effects independently of event publication.

## Completion and persistent reading

GameStatus shows a completion paragraph whenever `isWon(game)` is true. A newly won game can give it the celebration class; an imported completed game shows it statically. That paragraph is persistent reading content containing the final moves and time.

The winning turn's feedback already contains the match and win in one result. The status paragraph does not need to separately announce a matched pair, then publish a second completion sentence. This avoids having two updates compete at the most significant turn in the game.

A completed snapshot instead publishes its load outcome, because import is the event that just occurred. The game is visibly complete, but no new card match happened. This distinction preserves a useful account of what the user actually did.

## Automated evidence

`session.test.ts` checks that first reveal, mismatch closure and repeated mismatch events affect announcement identity as expected. It also checks import outcomes and completion transitions without involving the browser.

`tests/announcements.e2e.test.ts` observes DOM mutations in the status paragraph. It resolves a mismatch, moves focus, runs the mismatch interval and repeats the same attempt. The expected result history contains the mismatch sentence once for each resolved turn, with no extra result from movement or closure.

The same test submits each snapshot load kind and each invalid-load kind twice, checking the publication history and the visible load notice. `tests/status-controls.e2e.test.ts` checks that the result remains beside the board during large-phone play and that the reproduction panel has no competing result role.

The accessibility journey reads Chromium's tree for the polite and atomic properties and the result text at each turn. That establishes exposure in the tested runtime. Spoken scheduling and verbalization are assessed in user acceptance. The repository records spoken review as user acceptance.

## Diagnosing a repeated or missing result

A missing second identical result suggests checking event identity before changing the sentence. A repeated result on every clock tick suggests checking whether routine advancement touches the publication fields. A load notice visible near the textarea but absent from event output suggests checking whether the controller used `notice` or only changed local text.

For a report, the useful sequence is the action, feedback string, announcement number and observed mutations. That evidence can show whether the session failed to publish, React had no relevant change or the browser exposed the expected update but a spoken review behaved differently. The policy gives a single publication boundary; diagnosis follows it from the event to the paragraph rather than adding more announcers around the page.

# Native controls guide

This page explains the native HTML elements used by Neon Pairs and the behavior they supply to the interface.

The source combines React event wiring with browser controls. It does not draw input controls on canvas or implement a replacement select menu. The resulting code leaves common editing, activation and disclosure behavior with the browser while keeping game decisions in the session and core.

## The current element choices

| Element | Use in the game | Application responsibility around it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `button` | Cards and actions | Decide what the activation changes |
| `select` with `option` | Grid size | Supply supported sizes and start a deal |
| `label` | Grid size and text fields | Associate visible names with field ids |
| `input` | Board-code draft | Read and validate the submitted code |
| `textarea` | Snapshot draft and export | Hold text and pass it to the snapshot decoder |
| `form` | Board-code submission | Prevent navigation and handle the result |
| `details` with `summary` | Reproduction disclosure | Supply content and layout |
| `dl` with `dt` and `dd` | Current game statistics | Derive the displayed values |

These choices describe the current DOM. Policies for other kinds of content are documented in [Dialog policy](dialog-policy.md) and [Tables policy](tables-policy.md), without implying that those elements already appear in Game.

## Buttons unify activation

Card renders a native button with `type="button"`. Its `onClick` sends an index to the shared activation path. Enter and Space can activate the same control through normal button behavior, so there is no separate keydown implementation of reveal.

The board's keydown handler only handles plain arrows with a navigation target. It does not call activation for Enter or Space and then also allow a native click. That avoids two paths processing one keyboard action. The game's pure activation guard still decides whether the card is eligible.

Action buttons outside the board use explicit types too. The Board code loader is `type="submit"` inside its form. New Game, Restart, Export snapshot, Load snapshot and Resume are `type="button"`. This makes submission intent visible in JSX rather than relying on where the browser happens to find an enclosing form.

A native button's semantics do not automatically implement ARIA-disabled behavior. Card uses `aria-disabled={matched}` while remaining focusable, and the game ignores matched activations. [Disabled state guide](disabled-state-guide.md) explains that deliberate split.

## The select keeps its native interaction

Controls renders a labeled select whose value comes from `game.size`. Each option comes from `GRID_SIZES` and has a numeric side length value with `NxN` display text. The browser supplies its dropdown interaction and option-selection behavior.

The component handles change by converting the selected value to a number and calling `newGame`. There is no local menu-open flag, active-option state or custom pointer hit testing. The controller still checks supported sizes, because native options are an interface aid rather than the only trust boundary.

The select inherits the shared font and panel colors through `.control`. Styling the border and background does not replace its role or its label relationship. The current CSS does not remove it in favor of an invisible field beneath a separately focusable drawn menu.

A successful board-code or snapshot load changes the actual game size, which flows back into this controlled select. The visible selected option therefore follows the model rather than a second UI-only size state. [Control bar](control-bar.md) covers that data flow.

## Text editing remains text editing

Board code is an input, and Snapshot JSON is a textarea. They retain selection, caret movement and browser editing operations. The textarea can resize vertically and receives readable export text without a clipboard permission dependency.

The card's `user-select: none` styling is scoped to `.card`. It does not disable selecting an exported snapshot. The code-field spell-check and autocomplete settings reflect its format-oriented use; the snapshot field disables spell checking as well. None of those attributes validates the entered data.

BoardCodeForm uses FormData and prevents the form's default navigation in `onSubmit`. Pressing Enter in the input reaches that same submission path. The snapshot tools instead use local React state and explicit action buttons, preserving multiline Enter behavior in the textarea.

Controlled and uncontrolled fields both appear here. Reproduction controls the textarea value with state. BoardCodeForm uses `defaultValue` on an input keyed by generation. Native element choice does not determine which React state pattern is appropriate. The intended draft lifecycle does; see [Reproduction panel](reproduction-panel.md).

## A disclosure is already an interaction

The reproduction panel uses details with a summary, starts collapsed and relies on native expansion. There is no handler toggling an `expanded` variable or emulating summary key activation. The CSS styles the panel and summary without changing their source order.

The summary's visible text supplies its purpose. The load notice and Resume live outside the collapsible body, so closing it does not hide the pause continuation action. This is a layout and component-boundary decision around the native disclosure, not a custom disclosure implementation.

A disclosure leaves the surrounding document operable and expands in flow. It is not equivalent to a modal overlay. That distinction matters when reading a feature description: choosing a different native element changes more than a border shape or animation.

## DOM cards and artwork

Board is a CSS grid of DOM buttons, and each visible face is an inline SVG child. Hidden cards omit the face component entirely. The button name comes from position, state and, when available, face description; the SVG is hidden from accessibility and cannot receive focus.

The face drawing is therefore not the input surface's semantic replacement. A user activates the button, not an independently focusable path inside the SVG. This keeps the artwork and interaction connected without requiring canvas coordinate mapping or an invisible parallel button list.

The matched check mark is also an aria-hidden, nonfocusable SVG. It reinforces state visually while the button name and disabled property express it through the control. [Card artwork](../visuals/card-artwork.md) and [Screen reader notes](screen-reader-notes.md) describe those channels more fully.

## Native elements still need application work

The browser does not know that a pair matches, that a snapshot import is paused or that a game replacement invalidates an old timer. Those decisions remain in `game.ts`, `session.ts` and `use-game.ts`. A correct native element can still call the wrong controller action.

Nor does a button automatically implement the board's remembered entry point. `useBoardFocus` supplies the tab-index pattern and arrows, while the browser supplies basic focus and activation. The scroll helper addresses a specific Chromium centering behavior rather than replacing all browser scrolling.

Labels and descriptions also need correct associations. A visible label next to an input is not sufficient if its `htmlFor` points elsewhere. A load notice remains useful because the buttons reference its actual id. Native semantics reduce custom behavior, but they do not excuse checking the JSX relationships.

The same applies to CSS. Minimum height, shrinking fields, wrapping rows and visible outlines are explicit styles. A native input can still overflow a narrow page if its sizing constraints are wrong. [Form layout guide](form-layout-guide.md) and [Target size policy](target-size-policy.md) cover those aspects.

## Why alternatives would carry more work

Replacing the select with a drawn menu would move option navigation, expansion, selection and focus handling into application code. Replacing summary with a styled generic container would require recreating its activation and expanded-state exposure. Those are concrete costs even if the replacement initially resembles the current design.

A canvas board would also need a separate way to expose each card's position, name, state and focus behavior. The current DOM makes those properties inspectable directly. This is the benefit behind the existing choice, not a claim that native elements alone solve every accessibility issue.

The source does not contain a component library or a custom form abstraction that all new controls must use. Shared labels and CSS are small local tools. [ADR 006](../decisions/adr-006-native-controls.md) is the decision reference, while [Architecture](../architecture/architecture.md) explains the separation between browser effects and pure game behavior.

## Evidence in review

The controls tests locate fields and buttons by names and roles, inspect native option values and check selectable export text. Keyboard tests rely on normal Tab exit and native button activation. The accessibility journey captures the browser's exposed control roles and states.

These checks are more informative than asserting only that a div has the right class. They verify the interaction surface that the player receives. At the same time, they remain browser and tree evidence, with spoken confirmation assigned to user acceptance in the repository README.

For a refactor, compare element type, explicit button type, field association, key handling and callback as a connected path. If a visual wrapper is the only intended change, those details reveal whether it also changed submission, tab order or mobile flex behavior. The native structure makes the comparison concrete.

# Disabled state guide

This page explains why some card activations have no effect while the controls remain focusable and usable for navigation.

The game separates control semantics, focus and game eligibility. A matched card exposes an unavailable state, but it stays in the board. A mismatching pair temporarily blocks further activation, yet arrows can still explore the same coordinates. These are deliberate differences rather than one universal disabled flag.

## Matched cards use ARIA state

`Card.tsx` sets `aria-disabled={matched}` on its native button. It does not set the HTML `disabled` attribute. When matched is true, the button remains available to programmatic focus and the board's remembered tab-stop mechanism.

The card's accessible name includes `matched`, along with its coordinate and face description. Its face remains visible, its border becomes the green palette color and a corner check mark appears. Matched cards retain full opacity. The state is communicated through text, semantics and visual treatment rather than by dimming the card until it is difficult to identify.

The click handler still calls `activate(index)` for a matched card. ARIA describes the state; it does not suppress native events. The actual game guard in `activateCard` checks `state.matched.includes(index)` and returns the same state. The session sees that identity and returns without publishing a new result.

This is an important code-reading boundary. Removing the guard because a button “is already disabled” would mistake an accessibility attribute for an event blocker. Conversely, adding native disabled would change focus behavior even if ignored activation still produced no move.

## Why focus remains available

The board uses one remembered card in the page's tab sequence. Arrow movement traverses coordinates without skipping solved positions. A match can therefore leave focus on its second card, and the next arrow still means the adjacent row or column.

If matched buttons became natively disabled, they would no longer participate in the same focus behavior. Remembered entry could point to an unavailable native focus target, and movement would need a different policy for skipping positions. The current input specification instead keeps the rectangular geometry stable.

A player can leave with Tab and return to the remembered matched card. Activating it again has no game effect. This is covered in `tests/keyboard.e2e.test.ts`, which checks the disabled attribute, continued focus and unchanged move count after another Space activation.

[Board keyboard navigation](board-keyboard-navigation.md) explains the tab-index pattern and edge clamping. The disabled state does not create a second movement algorithm or change the size of the board.

## A revealed first card is different

The first revealed card has state `revealed` and is not matched. It therefore exposes `aria-disabled="false"`. Activating it again is nevertheless ignored by the game's `SelectionKind.one` branch because `first === index`.

This is not inconsistent with the matched-card treatment. The first reveal is an intermediate turn state. The game waits for a different eligible position to complete the attempt, while the first card remains readable and focusable. The button name describes what the player can know, and the core determines whether this particular activation advances the turn.

There is no separate “selected but disabled” CSS class or native disabling operation for that card. A repeated click may keep focus there and apply completed-click scrolling, but it does not add a move, restart elapsed time or produce a turn result.

The same separation lets a player navigate away from the first card and return without changing selection. Focus is not stored in the `selection` union. A review that derives reveal state from the currently focused element would collapse two independent parts of the interface.

## Mismatch blocking is in the game

After two different faces are revealed, selection becomes `mismatch` with a remaining active interval. The core's mismatch branch returns unchanged state for every attempted activation until advancement closes the pair. The unmatched card buttons do not all acquire ARIA disabled state during this interval.

Movement and focus remain available. A player can inspect coordinates or prepare a next choice while the pair stays visible. Closing the mismatch does not force focus back to either revealed position. The game-state change removes their faces, while navigation memory remains where the player moved it.

The controller synchronizes active time before processing a card action. An activation arriving when the mismatch has already expired can therefore be processed after closure rather than being rejected against stale rendered state. The guard operates on current synchronized game state, not a CSS class observed a moment earlier.

The interval pauses while the document is hidden. That is a clock lifecycle behavior, not a mass change to card attributes. [Mismatch interval](../gameplay/mismatch-interval.md) and [Clock design](../architecture/clock-design.md) describe the timing model.

## Imported pause is in the session

Loading unfinished progress sets `session.paused`. `activateSession` returns immediately while that flag is true, before calling the core activation function. `tickSession` also rejects advancement while paused.

The Board does not receive paused as a prop. It continues rendering the loaded game's visible faces, matched states and navigation callbacks. Unmatched buttons remain semantically unmatched rather than becoming a new paused-card class. The load notice and Resume explain the paused session state outside the board.

A player can move focus while paused. Resume returns to the current remembered card before clearing the pause and removing its button. A snapshot with a pending mismatch then continues its remaining interval. A completed import is not paused and has no Resume button; all of its cards are already matched.

The automated accessibility journey explicitly checks that a paused unfinished import does not mark unmatched cards disabled. This is stronger than assuming paused and disabled are interchangeable words. [Reproduction panel](reproduction-panel.md) describes the visible continuation controls.

## Deal and text controls stay usable

New Game and Restart are available during ordinary play, mismatch waiting and imported pause. Their controller operations replace the game and clear the old session context. There is no busy-state branch disabling them while a timer is active.

The reproduction actions also remain available. An invalid draft is submitted for validation rather than causing its load button to become disabled before the user can request a result. Export reads current progress without replacing the game. A valid load can replace a paused or active position through the same validated boundary.

The current forms do not use `required`, a disabled submit button or `aria-invalid` as their validation mechanism. Their native length limits constrain editing, and the controller reports invalid content on action. [Error display guide](error-display-guide.md) traces those outcomes and the preservation of drafts.

This describes the existing controls, not a new general rule that every possible action in a future feature is always enabled. The relevant question in review is which layer owns the reason an action cannot change state, and whether the element's semantics and focus behavior match that reason.

## Rendering, counters and no-op actions

Core activation returns the original object for invalid indices, matched positions, repeated first positions and mismatch blocking. The session preserves identity when the core does. That lets the surrounding controller avoid committing a new state for an ignored action.

Synchronization can still advance elapsed time before the ignored activation is considered. Seeing Time change around a no-op click does not mean the click added a move. The move count changes only when a second eligible card resolves an attempt, subject to its cap.

At completion, every index is matched, so further card activation follows the matched guard. The final clock stays stopped because advancement checks `isWon`. There is no extra completed-overlay element that captures clicks above the board.

These details help distinguish a correct ignored action from a lost input. A click on a hidden eligible card in a closed active game should reveal it. A click on a matched card should not change the turn. Both can deliver the same native event; their game-state eligibility differs.

## Review evidence

The useful checks pair an input with both its state effect and its focus effect. The keyboard test checks matched inactivity while focus remains. The input-contract test checks hidden controls' exact ARIA attributes. The accessibility journey checks matched disabled exposure and paused unmatched exposure. Session unit tests check paused activation and advancement independently of the DOM.

A defect report can name the card coordinate, its visible state, session pause status, selection kind and expected counter change. That information reveals whether the problem belongs to native focus, ARIA exposure, controller timing or core eligibility. Treating every ignored input as the same disabled-control problem would hide those distinctions.

# Dialog policy

This page records the confirmation policy for leaving unfinished work and its relationship to the game's existing actions.

The current source contains no dialog component, native dialog element or leave-work handler. New Game, Restart, board-code loading and snapshot loading call the controller directly.

## The confirmation boundary

A confirmation is useful only when it corresponds to a real decision about abandoning work. Its content and focus need to make the conservative path understandable before the player commits to leaving. Leaving unfinished work asks first in a native dialog element with two buttons, Keep playing and Leave. Keep playing takes focus when it opens, and Escape keeps playing. The decision is about the unfinished work being left; opening a disclosure to inspect a code is not itself that decision.

There is no third action specified by this policy. In particular, the existing snapshot exporter does not turn this confirmation into an automatic save workflow. Export is a separate user action with a text result. A feature that uses the confirmation can draw on that distinction without presenting an unsaved draft as if it had already been preserved.

The policy does not define which future feature owns a leave route or a new navigation screen. Those boundaries have to be visible in the feature's actual code. The current page has no router and no alternate play screen. [Focus policy](focus-policy.md) covers orientation when a feature introduces a main-area replacement.

## What the present controls actually do

`Controls.tsx` renders New Game and Restart as native buttons. Their callbacks in `use-game.ts` reset the clock adapter and commit a replacement game. They do not consult `started`, Moves, Pairs or a dialog result before doing so. The existing game replaces immediately when those buttons are used.

BoardCodeForm validates before replacing. Its `loadBoard` callback returns false for invalid input and true after successful replacement. Snapshot loading decodes the whole draft before replacing as well. These paths protect against invalid external data; they are not implementations of a leave confirmation.

The native `details` panel is also not a modal. It expands in document flow and leaves the rest of the page operable. Calling its summary a dialog trigger would misdescribe both the DOM and its focus behavior. [Reproduction panel](reproduction-panel.md) documents the actual disclosure.

This distinction matters during incremental work. A new dialog in one feature does not silently change the semantics of every old control. When reading a change, follow the event handler to see whether it reaches a confirmation boundary, a parser, or the replacement directly. Similar visual labels do not establish the same lifecycle.

## Native behavior and application decisions

The policy names a native element because the interface already relies on browser semantics for buttons, forms, selects and details. A dialog has a different interaction boundary from an ordinary panel. Its opening, cancellation and closing need to be considered as a coherent interaction rather than a div painted over the board.

Using the element alone does not decide what leaving means for a game. The application still owns the transition that discards or replaces state. In the current implementation, that transition is represented by controller operations and `replaceGame`. Visual disappearance of an overlay is not evidence that a session was replaced, just as visual appearance is not evidence that play was paused.

The distinction between cancellation and commitment is observable in game state. Continuing leaves the same deal, revealed selection and counters available. A committed departure may dispose of or replace the session, depending on the feature. The current game has no dialog-specific storage write or serialized marker.

No dialog state exists in `Session`. Its fields are `game`, `paused`, `generation`, `feedback`, `loadNotice`, `announcement`, `celebration` and `preferences`. The existing `paused` flag specifically represents unfinished snapshot import. Reusing that flag for a new overlay without considering its other consumers would also affect Resume and load notices.

## Timing questions exposed by an overlay

A mismatch stores its remaining active milliseconds in game selection. The session clock advances it when the page is visible and the imported-pause flag is clear. Merely placing a dialog above the board is not one of those conditions in the current source.

Consequently, there is no existing rule here that opening a confirmation pauses the elapsed clock or mismatch. A feature implementation needs to be read for its actual timing behavior rather than assuming that every modal surface freezes play. [Clock design](../architecture/clock-design.md) and [Mismatch interval](../gameplay/mismatch-interval.md) explain the established clock model.

Replacement does have a well-defined lifecycle today. `clock.reset()` and the session generation prevent old pending updates from affecting a replacement game. If a leave decision leads to that existing path, stale-timer protection still belongs to the session. The dialog does not need to know the two selected card indices to implement that protection.

The period between opening and making a decision is therefore worth observing in review. It can expose accidental differences between the visual state, current game state and timers. The observation is useful even when the feature's intended behavior is simply to preserve the current clock semantics.

## Focus ownership

Opening the confirmation establishes a temporary interaction context. The policy above states its initial focus and cancellation result. That avoids relying on DOM order alone to make the safe continuation choice the first keyboard target.

After a decision, the durability of the source control matters. Existing action buttons generally remain mounted after a deal replacement, while Resume removes itself. Game handles Resume by moving focus before the button is removed. That is a concrete example of a disappearing source, though it is not a dialog implementation.

A leave feature may keep or remove its trigger as part of its surrounding screen. Its focus return depends on which controls remain mounted. A review can inspect the final active element and its visibility.

The board also remembers focus independently of actual focus. Opening another surface would not, by itself, mean its last card index should become a selected turn. A player returning to the board still needs the distinction between orientation and activation described in [Board keyboard navigation](board-keyboard-navigation.md).

## Review notes for a proposed implementation

The most useful review evidence separates opening, continuing and leaving. A single screenshot of the open surface cannot establish which element is focused, whether Escape follows the continuation path, or whether the underlying controller already replaced the game before a decision.

A source trace can identify the first state-changing call relative to the decision. A keyboard trace can identify the active element at opening and after cancellation. A populated game, especially one with a pending mismatch, makes unintended early replacement visible. These are ways of observing the stated policy and existing game lifecycle, rather than additional product requirements.

Current browser tests establish focus retention on ordinary buttons, invalid draft preservation, Resume's transfer order and stale-timer protection. They do not establish a dialog journey. Any future report of dialog coverage has to point at the corresponding implementation and evidence, rather than citing those tests because they also involve focus.

The relevant background is [Native controls guide](native-controls-guide.md) for element choice, [Focus policy](focus-policy.md) for page orientation and [New game and restart](../gameplay/new-game-and-restart.md) for the existing replacement boundary. Together they make it possible to review a concrete leave interaction alongside the existing game lifecycle.

# Data exchange policy
This page explains which Neon Pairs data crosses a file or text boundary and how the existing formats relate to future exports.

The game has three exchange formats with deliberately different jobs. A board code identifies a starting deal. A snapshot describes a position on that deal. A replay describes activations on a logical timeline and produces a position when evaluated. Choosing the smallest useful format keeps a report understandable: a wrong shuffle needs a code, a wrong revealed state needs a snapshot, and a timeout ordering problem usually needs a replay.

The detailed contract is [Reproducibility](reproducibility.md). This page describes the boundary between those formats, browser session data and developer tooling. It is not an additional wire-format definition.

## Existing formats and new exports

The current snapshot and replay formats are JSON objects with numeric `version: 1`. The board code is a string whose prefix is `np1`. Their definitions predate the general policy for new JSON exports. Every new exported JSON object has a "format" of "neon-pairs/KIND", naming what it holds, and a whole-number "version", with its keys in alphabetical order at every level. Formats that already exist stay as they are. In particular, adding a discriminator to a version 1 snapshot would make it fail the existing exact-key check, and changing the board-code string into JSON would remove its usefulness in the Board code field.

There is an important distinction between naming a new exchange format and modifying a known one. `snapshot.ts` is still the authority for the fields of an exported snapshot. `replay.ts` is still the authority for a replay input. The general policy does not silently widen either accepted object. See [Format versioning](format-versioning-guide.md) for the compatibility decisions around those boundaries.

Current snapshot output is readable JSON produced by `JSON.stringify` with a two-space indentation argument. It writes fields in the construction order used by `encodeSnapshot`: `version`, `boardCode`, `matched`, `selection`, `moves`, `elapsedMs`, `started`. This order is not alphabetical. An importer accepts any object-key order when the required keys and values are present. The distinction matters when comparing documents: a change in whitespace or object-key order need not change the represented state.

## Choose the artifact by the question

| Question | Useful artifact | What it cannot establish |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Did two runtimes generate the same deal? | Board code | Which cards the player activated |
| Can another browser show this position? | Snapshot | The complete earlier action sequence |
| Does a click at the mismatch boundary get accepted? | Replay | The browser's real scheduling behavior |
| Does a loaded position show the right controls? | Snapshot plus browser steps | How that position was originally reached |
| Did a local best survive reload? | A storage-focused reproduction | An exported snapshot carries no best record |

A board code is short enough to copy into a report without a separate file. Its meaning is stable because the prefix fixes generation. A snapshot contains enough progress to avoid playing back a long game. A replay is the most explicit description of action order, but the browser does not currently record or load replay files through its reproduction panel. Developer tooling evaluates them through the core and CLI.

A screenshot may accompany any of these, but it does not replace their machine-readable information. A picture of two cards cannot tell an engineer the exact pending milliseconds. A board code plus an action sequence can distinguish a bad card layout from a bad state transition. The appropriate artifact depends on whether the disputed behavior is generation, state, time or presentation.

## What the exchange formats carry

A board code carries generation version, supported side length and seed. `generateBoard` derives the immutable deck. The result contains face identifiers in position order; the code does not carry artwork, card names or a language setting. Loading it creates a fresh hidden state with no moves and no elapsed time. The algorithm and literal example are documented in [Board code format](board-code-format.md).

A snapshot carries `boardCode`, matched position indices, a tagged selection, moves, elapsed milliseconds and the `started` flag, alongside its format version. It does not duplicate the deck. Pair count and completion are derived after loading. Omitting those derived values avoids accepting a record in which the supplied pair total disagrees with the matched positions. [Snapshot format](snapshot-format.md) gives the complete field and validation reference.

A replay carries `boardCode`, an ordered array of `{atMs, index}` actions and `endMs`, alongside its version. It starts from the hidden deal rather than from an imported snapshot. The action timeline advances game time before each activation. The final time is advanced even when no action occurs there. This is how a replay can describe a mismatch closing after the final click. [Replay format](replay-format.md) covers the timeline and diagnostic result.

None of these objects contains a browser storage key, a saved size preference, a per-size best record, a focus location or an animation flag. Those values have different lifetimes and authorities. A loaded board's size becomes the chosen size through session replacement; that is a browser consequence of loading, not a separate field in the artifact. A completed import is displayed without recording an import as a new played result.

## Browser text is an explicit boundary

The reproduction panel is a native `details` element with the summary “Reproduce a game”. It contains the Board code input and Snapshot JSON textarea. Editing either field only edits a draft. `Load board` or `Load snapshot` performs the actual load. This separation lets a player inspect and correct copied text without replacing a running game on each keystroke.

`Export snapshot` fills the textarea with a point-in-time representation. The player can select and copy that text manually. There is no dependency on the Clipboard API, no upload step and no account exchange. Export does not put the live session into the imported pause state. If the source game keeps running while the text is copied, the later source position may differ from the exported one.

The Board code control permits 32 characters and trims surrounding whitespace in `useGame.loadBoard`. The parser used inside JSON does not perform that trim. The Snapshot JSON control permits 65536 characters, while decoding separately enforces 65536 UTF-8 bytes. These are different measurements. A text field limit is an input affordance; the decoder remains the format boundary for programmatically supplied text too.

Successful load resets the board's remembered tab stop to its first position through a new session generation. Load and export buttons retain focus, with Resume handling its own disappearing-button focus transition. Focus is not serialized, so sharing a position cannot restore where the sender last tabbed. See [Reproduction panel](../interface/reproduction-panel.md) and [Focus policy](../interface/focus-policy.md) for interface details.

## Core functions and effectful adapters

The pure format functions operate on strings and game data. `parseBoardCode` returns size and seed or `null`; `decodeSnapshot` returns a reconstructed state or `null`; `readReplay` returns a final state or a classified problem. They do not operate browser controls, write storage or read files.

The browser adapter in `session/use-game.ts` decides when accepted data replaces a session. The CLI adapter in `scripts/replay-cli.ts` reads UTF-8 text and converts accepted replay results through `encodeSnapshot`. Pasting that output into the browser adds normal snapshot import behavior, including a pause for unfinished progress. The replay evaluator itself has no pause field.

## Trust and interpretation

All copied or loaded data is untrusted. “Valid snapshot” means that the object satisfies the documented state constraints, not that its claimed result has a verified play history. A hand-edited object can be accepted if its fields remain consistent. That is useful for debugging and does not provide evidence of a person's performance.

Replays give a more explicit history, but they still contain author-supplied actions and times. The evaluator applies normal rules, including ignored activations, and does not attest who supplied the file. There is no authentication or signed result in the current exchange model. Local best moves are local game records, not a remote ranking service.

A board code also reveals enough information for a developer to regenerate the whole deck. That is its purpose. The browser still keeps hidden face identity out of hidden-card DOM content. Those facts are compatible: the shareable deterministic deal is a debugging tool, while the ordinary board presents the information available during play. [Import safety](import-safety-policy.md) describes validation and replacement behavior in more detail.

## Following a reported disagreement

For a generation mismatch, begin in `src/game/deck.ts` and compare the literal vector. For a rejected position, follow `snapshot.ts` into `snapshot-selection.ts` and `saved-format.ts`. For an unexpected action result, follow `replay.ts` into `advanceGame` and `activateCard` in `game.ts`.

A useful report preserves the original artifact and says which boundary was exercised. “The CLI rejected this replay” and “the browser rejected the CLI's output” refer to different decoders. Keeping that distinction often removes an entire round of reproduction work.

# Format versioning guide
This page explains which versions Neon Pairs exposes and how to assess compatibility when its exchange behavior changes.

The current product specification is version 2.2. Board generation, snapshots and replays still use their original format versions. A product release and an exchange format answer different questions: the release says which application behavior was delivered; the format says how an artifact is interpreted. The package's `1.0.0` version is another independent value and does not select a decoder.

## The version map today

| Surface | Version marker | Source authority |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Starting deal | `np1` prefix inside the board code | `BOARD_VERSION` in `deck.ts` |
| Progress position | Numeric root `version: 1` | `SNAPSHOT_VERSION` in `snapshot.ts` |
| Action timeline | Numeric root `version: 1` | `REPLAY_VERSION` in `replay.ts` |
| Product behavior | Specification status 2.2 | Existing game specification |

The JSON version does not absorb the board generation version. A snapshot is version 1 and contains a separately parsed board code. A replay has the same layering. Its action semantics and its starting arrangement both matter, but they are represented by different fields.

This is why replacing a JSON `version` with a product release string fails. The current readers compare the parsed value directly with their numeric constant. The string `"1"` is also different from number `1`. There is no negotiation, version range or “closest supported version” branch.

## Compatibility follows the reader

An existing snapshot reader accepts exactly seven root fields and three exact selection shapes. An existing replay reader accepts exactly four root fields and two action fields. Adding an optional annotation may look harmless to its writer, but an unchanged reader rejects it. In these formats, an additive field is not automatically a compatible change.

Property order and whitespace are different. Both readers parse JSON before checking key sets, so a reordered object with the same values is accepted. Formatting can still cross the byte limit. An export style change can therefore be semantically neutral for small files and affect acceptance near a size boundary.

Accepted array order depends on the field. A snapshot's matched list is validated by membership and whole-face counts; export sorts it numerically. A replay's action list is chronological data with stable ordering at equal times. Sorting a replay action list to make output look tidy can change its result even if no timestamp changes.

The general policies for future exchange objects and field diagnostics are in [Data exchange policy](data-exchange-policy.md) and [Import safety](import-safety-policy.md). They are separate from the accepted version 1 wire definitions. Reading a policy page does not make the current decoder accept fields absent from its exact-key lists.

## A board prefix fixes more than a seed

The reproducibility specification explicitly ties `np1` to the generation algorithm and says that a generation change requires another version. That includes initial paired-face ordering, Park-Miller constants, rejection sampling and backward shuffle order. A different unbiased shuffle is still a different meaning for the same seed.

An implementation refactor that preserves every generated deck leaves that meaning intact. A change that silently produces different cards for an existing code breaks the artifact even if the code still parses. This is the most direct compatibility promise in the exchange model because a short board code appears inside both JSON formats too.

The current `parseBoardCode` supports one prefix. No older-prefix dispatch table, migration helper or multi-version generation registry exists. Future support cannot be assumed from the fact that the prefix contains a digit. [Board code format](board-code-format.md) documents the actual parser and vectors.

## Semantic changes can matter without a new key

A replay's meaning includes advancing time before activation, preserving equal-time array order and resolving a mismatch at its exact closing boundary. Reversing one of those operations would change a version 1 result without changing its object shape. Comparing field lists alone would miss the compatibility effect.

Snapshot meaning includes the lower move bound, the range of pending mismatch time, and the distinction between unstarted and started-zero-move states. Loosening a check can accept objects an older reader rejects. Tightening one can reject previously accepted files. Either observation is more precise than calling the change “validation cleanup”.

Presentation changes have a different scope. Redrawing a face while preserving its numeric matching identity does not alter the generated deck. Changing a visible load notice does not alter accepted JSON. Those changes may need interface or acceptance evidence, but they do not automatically change the exchange format's interpretation.

## What this code does with unsupported data

Snapshot decode returns `null` for an unsupported version; replay read returns the `format` problem. The browser reports its existing generic snapshot failure, while the CLI explains that the file is not a version 1 replay with the exact root fields. Neither tries a best-effort fallback to another version.

There is also no automatic snapshot upgrade on page load. Active progress is not read from local storage. The user explicitly supplies a snapshot through the reproduction controls, and the current decoder accepts or rejects it. Preferences and per-size bests belong to a separate storage contract described in [Persistence overview](../persistence/persistence-overview.md).

The CLI's successful output is version 1 snapshot JSON even though its input is a replay. It does not preserve the replay's actions, and it does not stamp the output with the package release. This conversion can be used as evidence that a replay's interpreted final position is stable across an implementation change.

## Reviewing a proposed change

The useful comparison starts with concrete artifacts. A generation change can be checked against the published seed states and deck. A snapshot change can be checked against an initial position, a one-card position, a pending mismatch and a completed state. A replay change can be checked with equal timestamps, an exact timeout action, ignored activations and an endpoint beyond the elapsed cap.

Those are existing semantic boundaries. They reveal different failure modes: parser acceptance, reconstructed state, action order and output serialization. A test that only checks that JSON parses cannot establish compatibility at the latter three levels.

For an old artifact, ask whether the new reader accepts it and whether it represents the same position or actions. For a new artifact, ask whether the old reader accepts it at all. Exact-key formats often give different answers in those two directions. Recording the direction avoids a vague claim that a change is simply “backward compatible”.

The source currently supplies only single-version readers, not a general migration framework. Any future version handling will need concrete design work at the affected format. The existing boundaries remain the starting evidence: [Snapshot format](snapshot-format.md), [Replay format](replay-format.md) and [Reproducibility](reproducibility.md).

# Reproducibility
The reproducibility specification is a set of versioned formats that recreates Neon Pairs deals, progress and actions.

Status: spec version 2.2. Board codes, snapshots and replays keep format version 1.

A board code reproduces the starting cards. A snapshot restores a later position. A replay shows the actions that produced a position, so each format answers a different debugging question.

## Board code

- D01 - Use `np1-N-seed`, where `N` is a supported side length and `seed` is an integer from `1` through `2147483646`. Use decimal digits without leading zeros. The parser accepts exactly this form. Trim surrounding whitespace in the Board code control before parsing.
- D02 - Version `np1` fixes the generation algorithm below. The same code produces the same deck in every supported runtime. Changing generation requires another version. Time, animation and other random draws can't change this deck.

For example, `np1-4-1` describes a 4 by 4 board with generation version 1 and seed 1. It contains no progress.

## Generate

- D03 - Start the Park-Miller generator at `state = seed`. Each draw sets `state = (state * 16807) % 2147483647`. Use exact integer arithmetic. Seed 1 starts with states `16807`, `282475249`, `1622650073`, `984943658` and `1144108930`.
- D04 - Create the deck as `[0, 0, 1, 1, ...]` through face `N * N / 2 - 1`. Shuffle from index `N * N - 1` down to `1`. At index `i`, draw `j` in `0..i` and swap positions `i` and `j`.

For a draw with `b` possible results, set `q = 2147483646` and `limit = floor(q / b) * b`. Advance the generator and set `x = state - 1`. If `x >= limit`, draw again. Otherwise return `x % b`. This rejection step gives every result the same number of generator values.

The resulting deck for `np1-4-1` is `[6, 7, 0, 5, 2, 2, 0, 5, 3, 7, 1, 6, 4, 4, 1, 3]`.

## Snapshot

- D05 - Encode progress as a JSON object with exactly `version`, `boardCode`, `matched`, `selection`, `moves`, `elapsedMs` and `started`. `version` is `1`. `matched` is an array of matched position indices. Derive the deck, pair count and completion from these fields.

The `selection` object has one of these forms:

| `kind` | Other fields | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `closed` | None | No unmatched card is revealed |
| `one` | `index` | One unmatched card is revealed |
| `mismatch` | `first`, `second`, `remainingMs` | Two different faces await closing |

- D06 - Validate the complete object before replacing the game. Reject unknown keys. Require unique in-range matched indices containing whole face pairs. Selection indices must be in range and unmatched. A mismatch needs distinct indices with different faces and an integer `remainingMs` from `1` through `800`. Completion requires a closed selection.
- D07 - Require boolean `started` and nonnegative safe integers for `moves` and `elapsedMs`. Reject `elapsedMs` above `359999999` and `moves` above `999999`. Apply the move cap to saved best scores too. Require at least one move per matched pair and one further move for a pending mismatch. If `started` is false, require zero moves, zero elapsed time, no matches and a closed selection. A started game with zero moves requires one revealed card. Import of unfinished progress pauses the clock and pending mismatch until Resume. Completed imports stay completed without a pause.

Illustrative snapshot:

```json
{"version":1,"boardCode":"np1-4-1","matched":[0,11],"selection":{"kind":"mismatch","first":1,"second":2,"remainingMs":300},"moves":2,"elapsedMs":1500,"started":true}
```

Importing this snapshot shows one matched pair and two different faces. Resume lets those faces close after another `300` active milliseconds.

## Replay

- D08 - Encode a single deal as `{version: 1, boardCode, actions: [{atMs, index}], endMs}`. Require exactly these fields and exactly `atMs` and `index` per action. Indices must be in range. Times are nonnegative safe integers. Action times must be nondecreasing. If actions exist, `endMs` must be at least the final action time. Equal-time actions keep array order.
- D09 - Start from the code's hidden deal. Advance active time to each action's `atMs` before activating its index, then advance to `endMs`. Resolve a mismatch whose interval ends exactly at an action time before that action. Apply the game rules to ignored activation too. Cap replayed elapsed time at `359999999` milliseconds as R07 requires. Action times and `endMs` keep the nonnegative safe integer range in D08.

Illustrative replay:

```json
{"version":1,"boardCode":"np1-4-1","actions":[{"atMs":0,"index":0},{"atMs":0,"index":11}],"endMs":800}
```

This replay ends with one matched pair, one move and `800` elapsed milliseconds. Replay timestamps use a logical timeline. The game's elapsed clock still starts at its first valid activation. Replay omits hidden-page and imported-pause time. A new deal starts another replay.

## Limits

- D10 - Limit snapshot JSON to `65536` UTF-8 bytes. Limit replay JSON to `1048576` UTF-8 bytes and `10000` actions. Reject malformed JSON and unsupported format versions. For snapshots, inconsistent data means a violation of D05, D06 or D07. For replays, it means a violation of D08 or D09. For board codes, validate D01. Validation checks these stated constraints, without requiring a reconstructed history of earlier turns. Invalid board codes and snapshots keep the current browser game. Invalid replay files are rejected by the CLI and game core.

These local formats and saved scores are untrusted input. Validation checks the state rules, not a verified play history. The game has no accounts or trusted leaderboard.

Turn and clock behavior is defined in [Rules](../gameplay/rules.md). Return to [Neon Pairs](../README.md) for the full specification.

# Persistence overview

This page explains the small amount of browser data Neon Pairs saves and the boundary between remembered preferences and an active game.

The game has one application storage key, `neon-pairs.preferences.v1`. Its value remembers the selected board size and the lowest completed move count for each size with a record. It does not contain a saved game. Reloading the page reads those preferences and creates a fresh deal at the remembered size. This is the most useful distinction to establish before investigating a report that something disappeared.

## The durable part of a visit

`src/game/session/storage.ts` defines the persistence data and its reader and writer. The in-memory `Preferences` interface has two properties: `size`, a number, and `bestMoves`, a read-only mapping from size strings to move counts. The writer adds `schemaVersion: 1` when serializing it. A representative stored value is:

```json
{"schemaVersion":1,"size":6,"bestMoves":{"4":9,"6":20}}
```

Here the next page load starts a new 6x6 game. The best displayed while playing that size is 20. Choosing 4x4 exposes the independent best of 9. There is no record for 8x8, so the status displays `none` for that size. The selected size does not have to be the only size represented in the score map.

The list of supported side lengths comes from `GRID_SIZES` in `src/game/deck.ts`: 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14 and 16. `DEFAULT_SIZE` uses the first entry, currently 4. A missing or rejected preference value therefore produces a playable 4x4 start with an empty score map. Storage is useful for continuity between visits, but the game does not depend on it to construct a board or resolve a turn.

See [Preferences store](preferences-store.md) for the exact validation and React effect. [Best score records](../gameplay/best-score-records.md) covers the gameplay meaning of the numbers rather than the browser mechanism that holds them.

## What remains in this page's memory

The active session includes the game, pause state, session generation, feedback, load notice, announcement counter, celebration flag and preferences. Only the preference portion reaches `writePreferences`. The session's game contains the board description, deck, matched positions, selection, moves, active elapsed time and started flag. None of that game progress is automatically written to browser storage.

This has several visible consequences:

- Reloading during a mismatch produces a fresh board rather than restoring the two exposed cards.
- Reloading after a win retains an eligible best, but it does not restore the completed board or its banner.
- Restart repeats the current deal only within the active session. Reload is a separate operation and starts a fresh deal.
- A loaded snapshot can change the remembered size even though its matched cards and elapsed time will disappear on reload.
- A draft in the reproduction controls is not a browser save. Typing text there does not itself create a durable preference change.

These are ordinary consequences of the data boundary, rather than separate recovery modes. A screenshot showing a nonzero move count says nothing about whether that count was stored. A storage dump showing a best says nothing about the last board code. For progress transfer, the explicit snapshot controls are the relevant tool; see [Snapshot format](../sharing/snapshot-format.md) and [Reproduction panel](../interface/reproduction-panel.md).

## When preferences change

`useGame` obtains a browser store once through `useState(browserStore)`. Its session initializer calls `readPreferences(store)` and then `initialSession(freshBoardCode(preferences.size), preferences)`. The size affects board creation, while the score map is retained alongside the new game. `useSavedPreferences(store, session.preferences)` connects that object to the writer after rendering.

Replacing a game goes through `replaceGame` in `src/game/session/session.ts`. It makes a new preference object with `size: game.size`, preserving the existing score map. This path is shared by changing size, New Game, Restart, a valid board-code load and a valid snapshot load. Consequently, replacing a game can cause a preference write even when the selected size has not numerically changed. The effect follows object identity; it does not compare serialized strings.

Invalid board-code and snapshot loads take an earlier exit. They update feedback through `notice`, leaving preferences alone. A rejected draft therefore does not alter the last accepted size. The browser test `valid board loads save their size while invalid loads keep that preference` exercises this distinction with a valid 6x6 board followed by invalid text and a reload.

During ordinary turns, the session continues carrying the same preferences object. On completion through card activation, `activateSession` calls `rememberBest`. A first result for a size or a strictly better result makes a new score map and preference object. Equal and worse counts return the original preference object. Clock ticks and intermediate reveals change game state without scheduling preference writes merely because time or moves changed.

## Why the stored value stays small

The preferences answer two recurring questions: which size did this browser use, and what is its best completed move count for this size? They can answer both without retaining every attempt. There is no attempt log, record timestamp, saved deck, player identity, sound option or theme preference in the current schema. There is also no automatic snapshot written on every move or on page exit.

This keeps browser effects out of game rules. `rememberBest` is a pure transformation; the session decides when it applies, and the hook performs the browser write later. Storage denial cannot stop a match, because matching does not ask storage for permission or wait for a successful write. A page can remain fully playable with the store represented by `null`.

The small payload also limits synchronous work. `localStorage` uses a synchronous API, but this implementation serializes a compact aggregate instead of the whole active board repeatedly. It does not store artwork, assets or the distribution HTML there. Offline delivery comes from the built file, not from browser preference storage. [Offline delivery](../architecture/offline-delivery.md) describes that separate concern.

## Locality and lifetime

The storage belongs to the browser context and origin that opened the game. A second browser profile has its own data. A different HTTP port can put an otherwise identical build in another origin. Moving between direct disk delivery and a local HTTP address is therefore not a reliable way to carry preferences over. The technology specification uses a local HTTP origin for saved-preference checks because disk URL storage behavior varies.

The app does not synchronize preference changes between open tabs. Each tab reads its initial value and then writes its own in-memory aggregate. One tab can overwrite another tab's changes; the specification explicitly leaves several simultaneous game windows outside the supported journeys.

Browser policy, explicit site-data deletion and private-session cleanup can also end a stored value's lifetime. The app has no server copy from which to recover it. [Private browsing notes](private-browsing-notes.md) and [Storage quota notes](storage-quota-notes.md) separate these environmental issues from the application's own replacement behavior.

## Reading this group of pages

The existing preference representation is older than the feature-level storage conventions described in [Persistence envelope](persistence-envelope.md). The existing writer continues to emit the preference aggregate. Likewise, [Retention policy](retention-policy.md) concerns saved lists; the current best-score map is an aggregate, not an attempt list.

For failures, begin with the operation that failed. Accessing `window.localStorage`, reading a key, parsing its string and writing a replacement are distinct stages. [Storage failure policy](storage-failure-policy.md) covers unavailable storage and the feature behavior built around it. [Corrupt data policy](corrupt-data-policy.md) covers values that can be read but cannot be accepted. Both cases lead to usable in-memory state, but their evidence and timing differ.

[Storage testing guide](storage-testing-guide.md) maps the unit and browser evidence to the boundary being investigated. It also explains how a served origin, isolated context and operation-specific store double make a persistence report reproducible.
