# Announcements policy

This page describes how event feedback is published, repeated and kept separate from routine game rendering.

The game has many visible updates, but only some represent a new result. A clock tick is a changing value; resolving a turn is an event. Treating those as the same kind of update would make a memory game noisy and would bury the information a player needs after selecting two cards.

## Publication point

`Game.tsx` places the game result between the board instructions and the Board itself. Its paragraph has `role="status"`, `aria-live="polite"` and `aria-atomic="true"`, with the current feedback inside a span. The page has exactly one live region, the status paragraph in Game.tsx. New status text, such as whose turn it is, goes through that region. The current game publishes pair results and load outcomes there; it has no turn-owner feature.

The paragraph remains mounted while its content changes. It is inside `.game-result`, which has a minimum height of `56px`, flex alignment and margins. The wrapper reserves a readable area near the board without making the scrollable card content itself the announcement source.

Polite publication allows the browser and assistive technology to schedule the result around other speech. Atomic content indicates that the paragraph's result is treated as a complete update rather than an isolated changed number. These attributes express the intended exposure; the actual spoken experience still needs user acceptance with a screen reader.

## Session data behind the paragraph

The session owns `feedback` and an integer `announcement`. Game renders `<span key={session.announcement}>{session.feedback}</span>`. Updating the key replaces the child span even when its text is identical to the preceding result. This gives repeated events a DOM change without adding a hidden counter to the spoken text.

The counter is event identity, not a statistic presented to the player. It does not track moves, matched pairs or elapsed seconds. A failed load can advance it without adding a move, while the first card reveal changes game state without advancing it.

A broad render counter would be wrong for this job. Session renders occur for time and selection changes that should not repeat the last turn result. The explicit event field makes the distinction inspectable in `session.ts` and `use-game.ts`.

## Turn results

`activateSession` calls the pure `activateCard`. If the game object is unchanged, it returns the current session. If the result has selection kind `one`, it returns the updated game without changing feedback or announcement identity. That covers the first eligible reveal.

After the second eligible reveal, the result is either a mismatch or a match. The session builds the appropriate text and increments `announcement`. Completion is checked at this same boundary, so the winning match gets a combined result rather than two competing event publications.

| Result | Text produced by the session |
| --- | --- |
| First matched pair | `Pair found. 1 pair matched.` |
| Later nonfinal pair | `Pair found. M pairs matched.` |
| Mismatch | `No match. Cards close after a short pause.` |
| Winning pair | `Pair found. All pairs found in N moves and time.` |

Here `M` and `N` are replaced with the actual counts, and `time` is the output of `formatElapsed`. The singular branch is based on `game.matched.length === 2`. The final branch takes precedence over the nonfinal pair count.

A card's accessible name also changes when it reveals or matches. That is the focused control describing its own state, not a second turn-result producer. The text in the event paragraph summarizes what the two-card attempt achieved. [Screen reader notes](screen-reader-notes.md) follows those two sources in a complete game.

## Consecutive identical results

Two misses in a row produce the same sentence. Updating only a string state can leave the DOM text unchanged, which gives no new mutation for the second event. The keyed span avoids relying on a different visible sentence to distinguish them.

The current sequence is concrete. Initial feedback is empty. Revealing index 0 on `np1-4-1` changes selection to `one` without publishing. Revealing index 1 produces a mismatch and advances the event identity. After the interval closes, choosing those two indices again produces the same text with a later identity.

The counter advances once for each resolved attempt in that sequence, not once for each card action or timer update. A third activation during the mismatch is ignored by the game and leaves the event unchanged. The same is true of a repeated activation on the first revealed card.

There is no temporary blanking timeout between identical results. The implementation does not clear text, wait a guessed number of milliseconds and restore it. That avoids adding announcement timing to the game clock or introducing a second lifecycle that can outlive a replacement game.

## Changes that stay quiet

`tickSession` advances the game and returns a new session with that game, leaving feedback and announcement fields intact. Mismatch closure is part of this advancement. It does not publish a new “cards closed” result. The earlier mismatch sentence already told the player that closure would follow a short pause.

Arrow movement is local board focus state. It does not call the session feedback path. Clock renders update Time in GameStatus, while card memoization prevents unchanged cards from rendering again. Neither operation is a new turn result.

New Game and Restart call `replaceGame` with `imported: false`. That replacement clears the prior feedback and load notice while keeping the announcement number. A successful board-code load follows the same replacement path. These operations clear old context; the current source does not add a success sentence for a board-code load.

Clearing text is still a DOM change and may appear in a mutation trace as an empty result. It is different from republishing a turn sentence. The accessibility journey's expected record includes the new-game clearing event, so a raw count of every mutation is not a substitute for reading what each event contains.

## Load outcomes share the publication path

The controller's `notice(feedback)` helper assigns both `feedback` and `loadNotice`, then increments `announcement`. Invalid Board code publishes `Invalid board code.`; invalid Snapshot JSON publishes `Invalid snapshot.`. Repeating the same invalid submission is a new load attempt and advances the identity again.

For valid snapshot import, `replaceGame(..., true)` increments the identity and publishes either `Loaded snapshot. Select Resume to continue.` or `Loaded completed snapshot.`. The former corresponds to a paused unfinished game, the latter to completed progress. Valid board-code loading does not use the imported-snapshot branch.

Reproduction also renders `loadNotice` in its ordinary paragraph with id `load-notice`. The load buttons reference it through `aria-describedby`. That keeps the outcome visible beside the text tools and associates the description with their actions without creating another event publisher in that panel.

Resume clears feedback and loadNotice without increasing the event identity. It also transfers focus to the board before its button disappears. [Reproduction panel](reproduction-panel.md) and [Focus policy](focus-policy.md) describe those effects independently of event publication.

## Completion and persistent reading

GameStatus shows a completion paragraph whenever `isWon(game)` is true. A newly won game can give it the celebration class; an imported completed game shows it statically. That paragraph is persistent reading content containing the final moves and time.

The winning turn's feedback already contains the match and win in one result. The status paragraph does not need to separately announce a matched pair, then publish a second completion sentence. This avoids having two updates compete at the most significant turn in the game.

A completed snapshot instead publishes its load outcome, because import is the event that just occurred. The game is visibly complete, but no new card match happened. This distinction preserves a useful account of what the user actually did.

## Automated evidence

`session.test.ts` checks that first reveal, mismatch closure and repeated mismatch events affect announcement identity as expected. It also checks import outcomes and completion transitions without involving the browser.

`tests/announcements.e2e.test.ts` observes DOM mutations in the status paragraph. It resolves a mismatch, moves focus, runs the mismatch interval and repeats the same attempt. The expected result history contains the mismatch sentence once for each resolved turn, with no extra result from movement or closure.

The same test submits each snapshot load kind and each invalid-load kind twice, checking the publication history and the visible load notice. `tests/status-controls.e2e.test.ts` checks that the result remains beside the board during large-phone play and that the reproduction panel has no competing result role.

The accessibility journey reads Chromium's tree for the polite and atomic properties and the result text at each turn. That establishes exposure in the tested runtime. Spoken scheduling and verbalization are assessed in user acceptance. The repository records spoken review as user acceptance.

## Diagnosing a repeated or missing result

A missing second identical result suggests checking event identity before changing the sentence. A repeated result on every clock tick suggests checking whether routine advancement touches the publication fields. A load notice visible near the textarea but absent from event output suggests checking whether the controller used `notice` or only changed local text.

For a report, the useful sequence is the action, feedback string, announcement number and observed mutations. That evidence can show whether the session failed to publish, React had no relevant change or the browser exposed the expected update but a spoken review behaved differently. The policy gives a single publication boundary; diagnosis follows it from the event to the paragraph rather than adding more announcers around the page.

# Acceptance
Acceptance is a set of journeys that checks whether Neon Pairs meets its product requirements.

Status: spec version 2.2.

Finish a game, then start another one during a mismatch. The first journey checks play and completion. The second checks that an earlier timer can't change a new game.

## Play

Use these journeys with the requirements in [Rules](../gameplay/rules.md):

- Finish every supported size with complete pairs.
- Reveal one card twice, then reveal a different card. Check the exact move count.
- Match a pair, then miss a pair. Check the immediate match and the 800ms active mismatch interval.
- Hide the page during a mismatch, then return and finish its remaining interval.
- Start and restart during a mismatch. Check the cleared state and later timer updates.
- Finish games with better, equal and worse move counts. Reload and check the current size's best.

## Controls

Use pointer, touch and keyboard to follow [Input](../interface/input.md) and [Controls](../interface/controls.md). Check control labels, row movement, edge stops, native Tab exit and focus after each action. Check that hidden cards reveal no identity in the DOM.

Follow the keyboard journey in I17 and check its accessibility tree. During user acceptance, confirm spoken results with a screen reader, including consecutive identical results and the final match with its win.

## Appearance

Measure the layout and review all 128 faces against [Visuals](../visuals/visuals.md). Use a 44px grayscale face sheet to distinguish shape, marker and fill. Check 16x16 boards at both stated viewport sizes, full focus outlines and the equivalent zoom layout. Check reduced motion and the static completion banner after its single pulse.

Play through completion and reset while checking [Sound](../sound/sound.md). Every action stays silent.

## Reproduction

Check [Reproducibility](../sharing/reproducibility.md) with its example deck and replay. Check snapshot round trips and malformed input. Check the exact mismatch timeout before an equal-time replay action.

Load an unfinished snapshot, attempt input while paused, then Resume. Check its remaining active time and focus. Load a completed snapshot and check its static banner and unchanged best score.

## Delivery

Use a locked install, type check, unit tests and a fresh browser build as defined in [Technology](../architecture/technology.md). Open the resulting HTML directly from disk with network access blocked. Use a local HTTP origin for saved preferences.

Review the pure game functions, browser effects, file sizes and behavior placement against [Architecture](../architecture/architecture.md).

Back to [Neon Pairs](../README.md).

# Storage failure policy

This page describes how unavailable browser storage affects play and how saved-record features present that limitation.

The current game isolates storage failures from the active game. It catches errors while obtaining the browser store, reading the preference key and writing its replacement. The session can hold its selected size and best results in memory even when no durable write succeeds. There is no current preference-storage warning in the rendered game.

## Features with saved records

For a feature that presents saved records, the unavailable-storage state belongs near the data it affects. The active interaction can still use its current in-memory state even though later visits cannot rely on finding that state again. When browser storage is blocked, a feature keeps working in memory and shows "Progress won't be saved on this device." where its saved records would appear. This ties the explanation to the missing persistence rather than turning it into a failure of the whole game.

The preference adapter does not yet expose a blocked-status result. `readPreferences` returns a `Preferences` value in all cases, and `writePreferences` returns `void`. Neither return type carries an availability flag or failure reason. `Game.tsx` renders no preference-storage warning; saved-record features have separate failure feedback.

The existing status display remains driven by session state. A best achieved during a visit can appear there after a failed write because it is already in `session.preferences`. A visible best is evidence of the in-memory result; persistence across a later reload needs separate evidence. [Persistence overview](persistence-overview.md) describes the data boundary.

## Three browser operations can fail independently

The first operation is acquiring the storage object. `browserStore` in `src/game/session/use-saved-preferences.ts` returns `window.localStorage` inside a `try` block. If the property getter throws, the function catches the exception and returns `null`. A denied property getter is tested in `tests/browser-environment.e2e.test.ts` by defining a getter that throws a `SecurityError` before the game initializes.

The second operation is reading the key. A browser can expose an object whose `getItem` later throws. `readPreferences` protects that call and returns `{ size: DEFAULT_SIZE, bestMoves: {} }` on failure. Its optional call also accommodates a `null` store. A successful read can return no value, a malformed string or valid preferences; those are separate outcomes from a thrown read.

The third operation is writing a serialized replacement. `writePreferences` encloses both serialization and `setItem` in its `try` block. A thrown error is swallowed so it cannot interrupt play. A browser may accept reads and refuse writes, so successful startup does not establish successful saving. Quota exhaustion is one possible write failure; browser policy is another.

These stages explain why a single boolean based on the existence of the storage property would be a weak diagnostic. The game doesn't use such a probe. It attempts the real operation at the boundary and catches failure there.

## What the current fallback preserves

Storage failure does not bypass the game's own rules. Card eligibility, move counting, matching, elapsed time and completion still use their normal state transitions. The fallback affects the initial preference value and the durability of subsequent changes. It does not substitute a different deck algorithm or change how many moves a result takes.

After a denied startup read, the game starts at the default size with no saved bests. Choosing another supported size updates the active session. Completing a game can produce a best for that size in memory. New Game and Restart preserve those in-memory preferences because `replaceGame` copies the session preference object rather than rereading the browser store.

If storage remains unavailable, a page reload starts another session from the fallback. The earlier in-memory best is gone with the old page. This is the expected consequence of unsuccessful saving, even though play in the earlier page was complete and valid. A report that a score survived Restart but disappeared on reload is consistent with a write failure.

An imported unfinished snapshot remains usable under the same conditions. The snapshot text is decoded into game state, then the session handles pause and resume. That path does not require a successful preference write. The accepted board size may be retained only in the current session if the browser refuses the later save.

## No implicit retry service

The hook is a small effect:

```ts
useEffect(() => {
  writePreferences(store, preferences);
}, [preferences, store]);
```

There is no queue, timer-driven retry, backoff or unload handler. Another dependency change can cause another attempt, but the code does not poll for a browser setting to change. A returned `null` store is captured in state for the lifetime of that mounted game; enabling storage later does not replace that state value automatically.

If the captured store object exists and its methods change behavior, a later effect can succeed using the same object. For example, a test double can reject its first write and accept a later one. That is different from reacquiring a previously inaccessible property. Both cases can be modeled without making the game rules aware of browser error names.

The writer's lack of a success result also means the existing UI cannot distinguish a rejected write from a successful one. This is a deliberate limit of the current adapter, not a hidden confirmation mechanism. Any investigation that needs that distinction can observe the supplied store in a test.

## Read failure and corrupt data have different evidence

A denied read and an invalid JSON value both lead to fallback preferences. Only the former establishes that an operation could not be completed. A parse failure establishes that the browser returned text which the application could not use. Confusing the two can lead to a misleading message about browser settings when the actual issue is an edited value.

Similarly, a quota error does not mean the existing value is invalid. The old string may remain perfectly readable while the new result exists only in memory. A person may see a better current best and then see the older best after reload. That sequence is a useful way to reproduce a failed update without damaging a valid baseline.

[Corrupt data policy](corrupt-data-policy.md) follows the rejection branches in detail. [Storage quota notes](storage-quota-notes.md) explains why the small size of this app's own payload cannot establish that a shared origin has available space.

## Errors do not authorize deleting other data

The source only calls `getItem` and `setItem` for `PREFERENCES_KEY`. It has no storage-wide clear call, key enumeration or cleanup routine. `PreferenceStore` exposes only those two methods. The storage unit test explicitly seeds an unrelated key and checks that a preference write leaves its value intact.

This matters in shared local environments, where another page can occupy the same origin. A rejected preference write does not cause Neon Pairs to free space by deleting that page's values. The current fallback is simply to continue without a successful save. The app also does not switch to cookies, a server endpoint or another browser database after failure.

When reproducing capacity problems, a disposable origin or isolated browser context keeps artificial fill data away from a person's real preferences. That is a testing technique rather than an extra product recovery path. The test can remove the keys it created afterward; the shipped game contains no such test cleanup behavior.

## Evidence in the test suite

`storage.test.ts` uses a denied store whose read and write methods both throw. It checks that reading yields the default size and that writing does not throw. It also covers `readPreferences(null)`. This verifies the API boundary directly, without needing to configure an actual browser's privacy settings.

The browser environment test covers a different boundary: acquisition of `window.localStorage`. It installs the throwing getter before loading the game, loads a fixed board and matches a known pair. The harness gathers uncaught page errors and checks that none occurred. That demonstrates continued play after an acquisition failure, not persistence in that denied context.

These tests don't establish every browser policy or a physical disk limit. They also don't assert the saved-record feature notice described earlier. Reading the test title alone can obscure those limits; the actual injection point and assertions show what each test proves. [Storage testing guide](storage-testing-guide.md) extends that evidence into an investigation workflow.

# Focus policy

This page records focus behavior in the current game and the policy for a feature that changes the main screen.

Focus tells a keyboard user where input will go next. It is related to game selection but is not stored as part of a turn or snapshot. The current interface deliberately keeps deal-action focus, remembered board focus and card reveal state as distinct things.

## Existing page and future screens

`Game.tsx` currently renders one main area with an h1, deal controls, statistics, instructions, turn output, the Board and reproduction controls. It has no alternate-screen branch or screen-level h2 focus target. Replacing a deal remounts the board within that page; it does not replace the page with a different screen.

A feature that introduces a screen replacement has a different orientation problem from resetting a deck. When a feature replaces what the main area shows, focus moves to that screen's h2, which has tabindex="-1". This gives the new screen a programmatic landing place without adding that heading to ordinary Tab traversal. The current deal and load callbacks can still be understood on their own terms; they are not evidence that such a screen transition already exists.

The policy applies to the feature-level replacement described here. Expanding native details, updating statistics, closing a mismatch or displaying the completed-game paragraph does not currently create a new screen. Those operations retain the page structure and follow the existing behavior below. [Dialog policy](dialog-policy.md) covers a separate interaction with its own opening focus.

## Initial load is quiet

The hook `useBoardFocus(size)` initializes `focused` to zero. Board gives index 0 a tab index of zero and the other card buttons a tab index of minus one. This makes the first card available on entry, but no mount effect calls its focus method.

The browser's current focus therefore remains where it is at initial load. The page does not jump down to the board before a player has found Grid size or New Game. The board help paragraph describes how to enter and operate it. Its region uses `aria-describedby="board-help"` to associate those instructions with the board.

A remembered entry point is often described casually as “focus on the first card.” In this code that wording is incomplete. There is an entry point ready at the first card, while actual focus may be on the document, a deal button or another native control. Keeping those concepts separate prevents accidental mount-time focus stealing.

## Deal actions retain their location

New Game and Restart are native buttons that call the session controller. Neither callback moves focus into the board. After either action, a keyboard user remains on the button they used and can repeat the action or Tab toward the board. The size select uses its native interaction and likewise does not issue a board focus call.

The replacement increments `session.generation`, used as Board's React key. The newly mounted hook begins with a remembered index of zero. Thus the next board entry goes to the first card, even if the previous deal's memory was near its end. Actual action focus and future board entry are updated through different mechanisms.

A valid board-code load also increments generation. BoardCodeForm focuses its Load board ref on successful submission because its input is keyed by generation and will be replaced. That is especially important when the action was Enter in the input. An invalid submission keeps the input node and does not call the button ref, so correction can continue in place.

Clicking the load button starts with focus on that button, and an invalid click leaves it there. The distinction is based on the action's origin and successful input replacement, not on a general rule that all errors move focus into a field. [Error display guide](error-display-guide.md) follows those cases in detail.

## Remembered board focus

Board focus memory is a local hook state containing a card index. The `onFocus` callback updates it whenever a card receives focus. Board renders exactly that index with `tabIndex={0}`. All other cards remain programmatically focusable with `tabIndex={-1}`.

Arrow movement uses the DOM order of the deck and never changes game selection on its own. Tab and Shift+Tab are left to the browser, so the board is one stop in the page sequence rather than a trap. Returning to it finds the last focused card, even if that card is now matched.

Matched positions stay in the navigation geometry. A player does not need to relearn how many arrow presses separate two coordinates after a match. During a mismatch, focus can also move while activation is blocked. The same is true while imported unfinished progress waits for Resume. [Board keyboard navigation](board-keyboard-navigation.md) provides the calculations and edge behavior.

## Resume transfers before removal

Resume is the current exception to retaining focus on the action button. It exists only while `session.paused` is true. Clearing that flag removes the button, so leaving focus there would leave a disappearing target.

In `Game.tsx`, the local `resume()` function first calls `board.current?.focusRemembered()` and then `controller.resume()`. Board's imperative method focuses the remembered card with `preventScroll: true` and then brings it into view. Only after that does the controller clear the paused state and notices.

The ordering is observable. `tests/control-contract.e2e.test.ts` installs a focus listener and confirms that Resume is still present when the card receives focus. A visual assertion after the fact would not establish this timing. The focus-entry test also remembers a far card on a large imported board, scrolls away and confirms that Resume returns to that location with nearest alignment.

The remembered location after import is initially the first card because the import replaced the board. The player can change it while paused. Resume uses that current memory rather than the snapshot's revealed index or a hard-coded first card. A snapshot stores game progress, not the browser's last navigation location.

## Visible focus and scroll clearance

`game.css` defines `:focus-visible` as a `3px` white outline with a `2px` offset. `card.css` gives cards `scroll-margin: 6px`. This combination accommodates the ring when the card is brought to the edge of the scroll area.

The focus hook uses `card.matches(':focus-visible')` before scrolling in `cardFocused`. Keyboard movement can scroll immediately; pointer focus avoids moving a card under a held press. Board scrolls a clicked card after the click completes. The timing is part of reliable focus behavior, not only a visual polish detail.

`useNearestScroll` stores the board's last reported scroll position, restores it and then invokes `scrollIntoView` with nearest alignment. The source records the Chromium-specific reason: Tab or Shift+Tab can center a newly focused card before the handler runs. Starting from the prior view preserves the player's location as much as possible.

The helper leaves the outer page's scrolling to the browser. A review therefore measures both the card inside the board viewport and its visibility inside the window. A ring can be uncut by the board yet still sit partly below the window if the outer document did not move appropriately.

## Focus is not completion feedback

Winning does not move focus to the completion paragraph in GameStatus. The final card stays the current control, and the completed summary becomes available in document order. The final turn's feedback is published through the game's event output. The component does not force the player to leave the board simply because all pairs are now matched.

Likewise, a mismatch closing does not restore focus to either of its cards. Focus may have moved elsewhere while the pair was visible. The game-state update closes the faces while the user's navigation choice survives. An ordinary clock tick also leaves focus untouched.

These examples are useful when evaluating a proposed effect that focuses something whenever `game` changes. Game changes for elapsed time, first reveals, turn results and resets. An effect tied to that broad object would combine very different events and could interrupt typing or navigation. The existing code places its explicit focus operations at narrower action boundaries.

## Review evidence

The keyboard browser check covers Tab exit, remembered re-entry and matched-card focus. `tests/status-controls.e2e.test.ts` covers Enter submission from Board code. `tests/focus-entry.e2e.test.ts` covers nearest alignment and the switch from pointer use to keyboard arrows. `tests/layout.e2e.test.ts` checks outline clearance on large boards, including an interior card where container padding alone cannot protect the ring.

A useful focus report names the source control, action, destination and whether the source remains mounted. For example: “Enter in Board code loads 6x6, replaces the input and leaves Load board focused.” That is more precise than “load focuses correctly,” and it exposes why failure has a different result. [Interface review checklist](interface-review-checklist.md) gathers these journeys with layout and input checks.

For new screen work, the source review begins by locating the actual replacement boundary. For changes within the existing game page, it begins with the current action-specific behavior above. Screen replacement and the established board lifecycle have separate focus behavior.

# Form layout guide

This page explains the label, field and action arrangements used by the current controls.

The game has two kinds of control groups: the always-visible deal bar and the text tools inside Reproduce a game. They share native elements and the `.control` style, but their DOM and layout differ. This guide describes those differences so a markup refactor can preserve the actual interaction rather than just one screenshot.

## A map of the current groups

| Group | Markup and layout | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Grid size | Label and select in a flex row | `Controls.tsx`, `controls.css` |
| Deal actions | Two buttons in the outer wrapped flex row | `Controls.tsx` |
| Board code | Form with label above a field/action row | `BoardCodeForm.tsx`, `reproduction.css` |
| Snapshot JSON | Label and textarea in the panel's body grid | `Reproduction.tsx` |
| Snapshot actions | Two buttons in a wrapped flex row | `Reproduction.tsx` |
| Load outcome | Paragraph and conditional Resume in a wrapped row | `Reproduction.tsx` |

Only Board code is wrapped in a form element. The snapshot field is controlled React state in Reproduction, and its buttons explicitly call callbacks. Enter in a multiline textarea remains text editing rather than submitting the snapshot. Enter in Board code invokes the form's submit path.

## Labels are visible and associated

Grid size uses `htmlFor="grid-size"` and a select with that id. Board code uses `htmlFor="board-code"`, and Snapshot JSON uses `htmlFor="snapshot-json"`. The visible text supplies the fields' names; placeholders do not stand in for labels.

Board code also has `name="boardCode"` because its form reads that field through FormData. Its id serves label association; its name serves native form data lookup. Those are different roles, and changing one does not automatically update the other.

The snapshot textarea has no need for a FormData name in its current path because its value is held in React state and passed directly to `loadSnapshot`. Adding a name attribute alone would not turn its surrounding buttons into a form submission. [Native controls guide](native-controls-guide.md) explains the behavioral value of the current element choices.

The labels come from `control-labels.ts`. Keeping visible text in those constants does not change the label/field relationship. A review can inspect both the imported value and the actual id association, because a correct label string next to the wrong id is still a broken field relationship.

## Deal bar: horizontal until it wraps

The outer `.controls` container uses `display: flex`, bottom alignment, wrapping and a `12px` gap. The nested `.size-control` is a centered flex row with its own `12px` gap. On a wide layout, label, select and action buttons appear in one compact band above the statistics.

At widths up to 599px, the outer container stretches its children. The size group takes the full line and distributes its label and select with space-between alignment. The direct child buttons grow equally. The DOM order stays Grid size, New Game, Restart while the layout moves into two lines.

That stability matters for keyboard order. The CSS changes wrapping, not the tab sequence or source order. A visual rearrangement implemented by moving DOM nodes could affect where Tab goes; the present media query does not need to do that.

The group is not a native form. Changing the select calls the controller immediately. There is no Apply button or submission that combines the selected size with one of the deal actions. [Control bar](control-bar.md) documents those callbacks and what they replace.

## Board-code form: one label, one submission

BoardCodeForm renders a grid form with a `6px` gap. Its first child is the label. The next is `.control-row`, a wrapping flex container with a `12px` gap and bottom alignment. Inside are the input and the Load board submit button.

The input has `flex: 1` and `width: 16ch`. The preferred width reflects code-like text, while flex growth gives it available space. The shared control stylesheet sets `min-width: 0` for inputs and textareas so their intrinsic width does not force the page wider than its container.

The button is the form's explicit submit action. Its ref supports successful keyboard submission when the input is replaced. The form prevents normal page navigation, reads `boardCode` and calls the loader. The label stays outside the row so a wrapped button does not detach it from the field's visual group.

On the phone breakpoint, direct child buttons of `.control-row` get `flex: 1`. This selector is shared with the snapshot action row. A wrapper inserted between the row and a button would change this rule's target; a DOM cleanup can therefore have a mobile layout consequence even when desktop placement looks unchanged.

## Snapshot field: a larger editing surface

Reproduction's body is a grid with a `12px` gap and `4px 16px 16px` padding. The Snapshot JSON label and textarea are adjacent children of this grid. The textarea uses five rows, fills its available width and can resize vertically.

Export replaces its value with readable JSON. Import reads the current value. There is no automatic serialization on every game render, so the field can hold a draft while the player inspects cards or changes a deal. Its controlled state is independent of the board-code input's generation-keyed default value.

The two snapshot buttons follow in a `.control-row`. Both are `type="button"`, which makes the action semantics explicit even if the surrounding layout later changes. The current component does not depend on a textarea Enter press to decide which snapshot action to perform.

A manual copy workflow uses native text selection. The card-specific `user-select: none` rule does not apply to this field. Vertical resize and long structured text can make the disclosure tall, but the field remains an ordinary part of document flow.

## Shared control styling

`.control` sets minimum height, padding, border, radius, panel background, text color and inherited font. It is imported by both Controls and the reproduction components. The selectors for button and select add a pointer cursor, while the input and textarea selector handles shrinking.

The shared class does not create a universal component with all semantics and validation built in. A select still has native options, an input still has its own maximum length, and a textarea still has multiline editing. Their association, callbacks and error descriptions remain in the JSX.

`game.css` sets global border-box sizing and a system sans-serif font at `16px` with a `24px` line height. Form controls inherit the font instead of taking a separate browser default. The focus outline is shared through `:focus-visible`, so a form layout also needs enough space for that outline to be seen.

## Outcome text is outside the disclosure

The load notice paragraph and Resume are in `.load-status`, following details rather than living inside `.reproduction-body`. The row has a `12px` gap, wraps and reserves at least `56px` of height. The paragraph grows and has `min-width: 0`.

This placement makes a paused-load outcome usable after the disclosure closes. It also means a selector that searches only inside details will not find Resume or the notice. Tests deliberately inspect the adjacent load-status location. [Error display guide](error-display-guide.md) follows its content and the load buttons' `aria-describedby` relationships.

Turn output is elsewhere, near the board instructions. The layout does not put every changing sentence inside the form body. The distinction is useful when testing a large phone board: result visibility near the board and load feedback near the text tools are separate observations.

## Reflow and review examples

At a narrow width, the page should be read as a vertical flow of labeled groups rather than a fixed matrix of coordinates. The existing wrapped rows and shrinking fields let content determine height. The default board fits the narrow layout, while a large board confines its own overflow to its viewport.

A longer draft can remain in an input even when not all of its characters are visible at once; native text editing can scroll within the field. That is different from making the whole outer page wider. A multiline snapshot can expand or scroll internally without turning its label into a floating overlay.

The equivalent zoom test at `640x400`, device scale 2, checks readable controls, statistics and completion output. It also uses the snapshot tools at that constrained layout. `tests/controls.e2e.test.ts` verifies labels, native limits and selectable export text. Together the sources cover geometry and editing behavior without defining a new generic form framework.

For a proposed name field, these label and native-control patterns are relevant background, but there is no implemented name form to copy. [Text entry policy](text-entry-policy.md), [Name length policy](name-length-policy.md) and [Duplicate names policy](duplicate-names-policy.md) own its separate acceptance rules. The current interface has no name-field placeholder, character counter, error precedence or field order.

# Shared-device competition

This page explains the purpose, scope and implementation context of shared-device competition in Neon Pairs.

Competition gives a group gathered around one device a reason to return to the board together. It is intended for the small social setting: a family laptop, a tablet passed around a table, or a few people taking a break at the same desk. The interesting product question is how individual memory play becomes a shared occasion without losing the clarity of the existing game.

## Where the product stands

Neon Pairs includes a Tournament mode for four or eight people sharing one device. `src/game/Game.tsx` switches between the solo game and the tournament screen. Tournament rules live in `src/game/tournament`; the card engine remains shared and does not contain participant state.

Tournament play owns its current player, match results and board clock separately from the solo session. A participant starts a turn explicitly; both people in a match receive a fresh game with the same board code. A completed event appears in Past tournaments and can be exported or loaded as JSON.

The core game specification is version 2.2. The linked competition pages define the local bracket flow, stage sizes, match deal identity, result comparison and preference boundary. This overview summarizes the shipped mode without repeating those decisions.

## Why share a device

A shared screen makes the activity visible. People can talk about the artwork, remember a near miss and recognize the effort behind another person's finish. There is no remote opponent waiting behind a network connection, and no account setup between the group and the game. The game already has a compact delivery model: the built game can be opened from one HTML file.

Sharing hardware also changes what people expect. On a personal device, a result feels like part of that person's practice. On a shared tablet, the person holding it may have changed several times since the page opened. A familiar status area can therefore carry a different social meaning even when its numbers are technically correct. The distinction between a person's current attempt, the group's progress and the device's ordinary records is especially easy to blur.

Competition is useful when it gives those existing actions a context people can follow. It is less useful when the group spends more attention administering the session than remembering cards. This is why the research discussion concentrates on interruptions, orientation and the physical act of passing the device, rather than treating the bracket drawing as the whole feature.

## Three things people are following

An individual concentrating on a board is following card positions and remembered faces. Someone waiting nearby is following the social event: who is occupied, whether a finish is close and when attention will return to the group. The person explaining the game is following the application itself, often watching for a control that might replace the current position.

These perspectives overlap, but they are not interchangeable. A board full of exposed faces is meaningful to the current player. It gives a waiting person relatively little information about where the group is in its event. A compact event view can answer that social question, while the ordinary board remains the place where the player thinks.

The competition documents separate these subjects so that readers can find the relevant decision without extracting it from a long screen-by-screen walkthrough. [Pairing](competition-pairing.md) covers the relationship between entrants and the bracket. [Rounds](competition-rounds.md) covers event stages. [Boards](competition-boards.md) and [deals](competition-deals.md) distinguish the dimensions of a board from its actual arrangement. [Ties](competition-ties.md) and [scores](competition-scores.md) address results from different angles.

## A local social activity, with local evidence

The current project has no backend or account service. Its board codes and exported progress are useful for reproducing a situation, not for establishing the identity of a person who played it. That is a comfortable fit for a group that is physically present and can see what happened. It is a much weaker basis for claims about distant strangers.

The same limitation applies to development evidence. A replay can help an engineer understand a sequence of card actions. A screenshot can help someone understand what the group saw. Neither explains why a participant handed the tablet back early, or whether someone had been watching another person's screen. Those are observations about the setting, and they belong in the research account rather than in an assertion about the game engine.

[Reproducibility](../sharing/reproducibility.md) explains the existing technical tools. [Competition research](competition-research.md) describes local sessions and the limits of drawing conclusions from them. The two accounts answer different questions and are useful together.

## How the current code helps

The core already separates game data from presentation. `src/game/game.ts` contains card transitions and logical elapsed time. `src/game/deck.ts` contains board parsing and deterministic generation. Those files have no participant knowledge. That makes them a useful basis for discussing competition without embedding group administration into card rendering.

The browser session is a separate layer under `src/game/session`. It owns the bridge between the core and React, browser visibility, clock observations and solo preferences. `src/game/tournament` owns tournament progression and its independent active-time hook; completed history uses the separate `np3:tournaments` storage key. Tournament attempts do not change the saved solo size or best moves.

The board itself lives under `src/game/board`. Its card buttons and navigation code operate on positions. The status view receives a game and a best value; it does not discover an event or a participant. [Architecture](../architecture/architecture.md), [session module](../architecture/session-module.md) and [React boundaries](../architecture/react-boundaries.md) give the broader engineering context.

# Controls
Controls is a specification that defines the game options and reproduction tools in Neon Pairs.

Status: spec version 2.2.

You can start another deal, repeat the current one or load saved progress. Each control keeps the same label, so you can find the same action after a game changes.

## Deal controls

The main controls are:

- C01 - Label the native size select "Grid size". Give it options `4x4`, `6x6`, `8x8`, `10x10`, `12x12`, `14x14` and `16x16`, with numeric side length `N` as each value. After a successful board-code or snapshot load, select the loaded board's size.
- C02 - Label the fresh-deal button "New Game". It creates a fresh seed and keeps the current size.
- C03 - Label the repeat-deal button "Restart". It starts the same board code again.

- C15 - Place a "Tournament" button beside New Game. Open the shared-device tournament screen when it is selected. Its participant entry, bracket, result and history behavior is defined in [Competition](../competition/competition-overview.md).

Changing size, starting and restarting follow the session rules in [Rules](../gameplay/rules.md).

## Reproduction tools

- C04 - Put reproduction controls inside a native `details` element that starts collapsed. Give its summary the exact text "Reproduce a game".

The controls use the board-code and snapshot formats defined in [Reproducibility](../sharing/reproducibility.md). A board code starts a deal. A snapshot loads progress on a deal.

## Load a board

- C05 - Label the text input "Board code" and limit it to 32 characters. Show the current board code after a new deal, Restart or a successful load. Keep an edited draft when a card action changes the game.

- C06 - Label its button "Load board". Validate the entered code before replacing the current game with that deal's starting state.

For example, loading `np1-4-1` starts its hidden four-column board. Entering that code alone keeps the current game until you select Load board.

## Snapshot tools

- C07 - Label the textarea "Snapshot JSON" and limit it to 65536 characters. The parser also applies the UTF-8 byte limit in the snapshot format.

- C08 - Label the export button "Export snapshot". Fill the textarea with readable version 1 snapshot JSON that you can select and copy manually. Export leaves the game state and clock unchanged. It requires no Clipboard API.

Export `elapsedMs` and a pending mismatch's `remainingMs` as whole milliseconds. A pending mismatch always exports at least 1ms.

- C09 - Label the import button "Load snapshot". Validate the complete draft before replacing the current game. Load unfinished progress paused and show "Loaded snapshot. Select Resume to continue." Load completed progress as completed without pausing and show "Loaded completed snapshot."

- C10 - Show a "Resume" button only while an imported unfinished game is paused. Selecting it clears that pause. Unfinished play continues from the loaded state. While paused, block every card activation and allow board focus movement. On Resume, move focus to the board's remembered tab stop before removing the Resume button. A loaded completed game stays completed and shows no Resume button.

- C11 - On invalid input, keep the current game and the entered draft for correction. Show the exact status for that control:

| Control | Status |
| --- | --- |
| Load board | Invalid board code. |
| Load snapshot | Invalid snapshot. |

- C12 - A loaded completed snapshot keeps the win banner static and plays no celebration. Import doesn't write a best score. Resuming an unfinished snapshot and later winning records a local best under R10.

For example, loading a completed game with fewer moves than the saved best shows that game without replacing the saved record.

## Focus

- C13 - Keep focus on the button used for starting, restarting, loading or exporting. These actions don't move focus to the board. Resume follows C10 because its button disappears. The board's remembered tab stop follows the focus rules in [Input](input.md#focus).

## Replay

- C14 - Keep replay in the developer CLI and game core. V1 has no replay controls in the game UI.

Run `npm run --silent replay -- PATH` to read a replay file. On valid input, print only the final snapshot JSON to stdout and exit 0. On invalid input, print nothing to stdout, write a message to stderr and exit nonzero.

The complete game pack starts in [Neon Pairs](../README.md).

# Source layout

This page is a map of the current Neon Pairs source tree and the responsibilities of its files.

Paths here are relative to the project root. They describe authored source and configured outputs. [Module layout policy](module-layout-policy.md) explains placement decisions; this page is for finding the implementation.

## Entry and project root

`index.html` contains the document metadata, the `root` element and the development module entry `/src/main.tsx`. It declares English, a responsive viewport, the theme color `#090B14` and the title Neon Pairs. The source HTML references a module; the production HTML is assembled by Vite and the single-file plugin.

`src/main.tsx` looks up the root, throws `Missing application root.` if it is absent and renders `<Game />` under React `StrictMode`. There is no second application page or router mounted beside it. The game begins at `src/game/Game.tsx`.

The root also holds `package.json`, `package-lock.json`, four compiler configuration files, three Vite configurations and `vitest.config.ts`. `.prettierrc.json` configures formatting; `.prettierignore` and `.gitignore` identify generated or local work. The README records setup, commands, delivery, replay and the named runtime evidence.

## Game composition

`Game.tsx` calls `useGame`, passes session values and controller actions into the solo UI, and imports `game.css`. It also selects the shared-device Tournament screen; solo session time is suspended while that screen is open.

Its one extra coordination operation is Resume. It asks the board's imperative ref to focus the remembered card, then calls the controller's resume action. That keeps the DOM focus handoff outside the core state. `Board` is keyed by `session.generation`, so a replacement remounts the board's local state.

`game.css` defines root colors and spacing values, system typography, page geometry, global focus styling and the reserved turn-feedback area. The more specific board, control and status rules live beside their components. [CSS organization](css-organization.md) records selectors and cascade relationships.

## Core modules directly under src/game

| File | What a reader finds there |
| --- | --- |
| `deck.ts` | Supported sizes, seed bounds, board-code parser and formatter, seeded shuffle and immutable board description |
| `selection.ts` | The closed, one-card and mismatch discriminated union |
| `game.ts` | `GameState`, caps, creation, victory, face-up positions, activation and logical advancement |
| `elapsed-time.ts` | Display formatting from elapsed milliseconds |
| `saved-format.ts` | Small shared JSON, object, key, integer and byte helpers |
| `snapshot-selection.ts` | Validation of matched positions and nested selection |
| `snapshot.ts` | Snapshot version and bound, serialization and complete-state validation |
| `replay.ts` | Replay limits, structured problems, ordered actions and final state |

These files use ordinary TypeScript functions and data. The core is not a React context or reducer hook. It can be imported by the session adapter and by the replay CLI without mounting the application.

`generateBoard` returns a frozen description with a frozen deck. `GameState` extends that description. Runtime progress is returned as new objects by transitions; ignored actions can return the existing object. This pattern explains why the board's memoized sets can survive clock-only updates.

## Core test files

`game.test.ts` checks card transitions and logical advancement. `completion.test.ts` finishes every supported size. `move-cap.test.ts` exercises play and records at the maximum move count. `elapsed-time.test.ts` covers the formatter and related elapsed behavior.

`deck.test.ts` checks parsing and generation. `deck-rejection.test.ts` references independently generated vectors for rejection-sampling boundaries. `game.fixture.ts` contains the example code, literal deck, pair positions, initial generator states and shared numerical specification vectors.

`snapshot.test.ts` and `snapshot-selection.test.ts` cover the outer state and nested validation. `replay.test.ts` and `replay-order.test.ts` cover replay acceptance and ordering. These files live near the rules even when a narrow regression deserves a different test filename from the principal module.

## Session directory

`session/session.ts` defines `Session`, the import notices and the pure session operations `initialSession`, `replaceGame`, `tickSession` and `activateSession`. It connects a game transition to feedback, completion state and preferences without itself calling the browser.

`session/use-game.ts` is the React controller. It reads initial preferences, creates the initial fresh board, keeps the latest session ref in step with state, exposes actions and composes the clock and saving hooks. Successful loads replace the game; failed loads publish notices. Exports and activations synchronize the clock first.

`session/browser-clock.ts` defines the 40ms scheduling interval and arithmetic over observed timestamps. `session/use-session-clock.ts` supplies observations, maintains visibility, schedules timeouts and removes pending work on effect cleanup. `session/browser-clock.test.ts` checks the arithmetic independently.

`session/fresh-board.ts` converts browser entropy into a valid board code, rejecting out-of-range candidates and an optional previous seed. `session/storage.ts` defines the preference key, version, default size, store interface, validators and best-score update. `session/use-saved-preferences.ts` obtains browser storage safely and writes changes in an effect.

`session/session.test.ts` covers state replacement, paused input, generations, repeated feedback events and completion handling. `session/storage.test.ts` uses in-memory and throwing stores to cover persistence decisions. [Session module](session-module.md) follows the exact call paths and state fields.

## Tournament directory

`tournament/pairing.ts` defines the four- and eight-player opening order and stage sizes. `tournament/rules.ts` owns event progression, same-deal turns, result comparison and winner advancement. `tournament/names.ts` processes and validates entered names.

`tournament/event-format.ts`, `event-shapes.ts` and `format.ts` encode and validate tournament JSON. `tournament/storage.ts` retains completed events under the tournament storage key. `use-tournament.ts` connects tournament actions to React, while `use-tournament-clock.ts` handles active time and visibility. `Tournament.tsx`, `TournamentSetup.tsx`, `TournamentExchange.tsx`, `TournamentLive.tsx`, `PastTournaments.tsx` and `Bracket.tsx` render entry, play, results and export/load controls. `tournament.css` owns the tournament layout.

The adjacent pairing, rules, names and format tests check the event data and import boundaries. `tests/tournament.e2e.test.ts` exercises the public controls, same-deal handoff, saved history and early leave in the built game.

## Board directory

`board/Board.tsx` maps the immutable deck into cards. It derives a face-up set and a matched set, obtains the focus hook, exposes a remembered-focus method and supplies the `--grid-size` custom property. It keeps the activation callback stable while calling the latest controller action through a ref.

`board/Card.tsx` is memoized. It renders a native button, obtains its class and accessible description from `describeCard`, renders the face only when supplied and adds a matched mark for matched positions. It delegates navigation and focus to callbacks from the board.

`board/Face.tsx` converts a face design into inline SVG primitives. `board/face-design.ts` maps one of 128 face numbers to shape, marker, color, fill style, coordinates and label. `board/card-state.ts` derives a card's closed, revealed or matched description from supplied presentation data.

`board/keyboard.ts` computes arrow-navigation targets with edge stops and modifier handling. `board/use-board-focus.ts` owns the remembered position and DOM focus calls. `board/nearest-scroll.ts` remembers the viewport scroll position so focus can use nearest alignment after Chromium's automatic focus scrolling.

`board/board.css` owns the scrolling board viewport and grid tracks. `board/card.css` owns the button, concealed back, revealed/matched surfaces, corner mark and card transition. The directory's `keyboard.test.ts`, `card-state.test.ts` and `face-design.test.ts` check the numerical and descriptive helpers. Browser tests observe actual focus, artwork and scrolling.

## Controls and status

`controls/Controls.tsx` renders the grid-size select, New Game, Tournament and Restart. It reads the size options from `GRID_SIZES`. `controls/control-labels.ts` owns the exact solo deal and reproduction control strings consumed by components and tests.

`controls/BoardCodeForm.tsx` renders the board-code field and submit button. Its input is keyed by generation, and successful submission moves focus to the load button because the old input is replaced. An invalid submission leaves the draft available for correction.

`controls/Reproduction.tsx` holds the snapshot textarea draft in local state, renders the details disclosure and export/load buttons, and shows the load notice and conditional Resume button outside the disclosure. It uses the game code and generation passed from the parent rather than reconstructing them.

`controls/control.css` defines the common control surface. `controls/controls.css` lays out deal controls. `controls/reproduction.css` lays out the disclosure, form rows, textarea and notice region.

`status/GameStatus.tsx` renders moves, pair progress, elapsed text, optional best moves and the completion paragraph. `status/status-labels.ts` owns statistic labels. `status/status.css` styles the statistic layout and completion treatment. Tournament play hides the ordinary best statistic.

## Scripts directory

`scripts/replay.ts` is the command entry. It passes command-line arguments to `runReplay` and assigns the returned status to `process.exitCode`. `scripts/replay-cli.ts` handles one input path, caller-directory resolution, file reads, human-readable stderr failures and final snapshot output. `scripts/replay.test.ts` exercises the executable in child processes.

`scripts/source-files.ts` recursively reads ordinary files from a supplied folder and rejects links or special entries. `scripts/source-audit.test.ts` inspects packages, compiler settings, source length, unsafe constructs and selected effect boundaries. `scripts/source-conventions.test.ts` checks recognized exports/imports, yes-or-no naming, test names and environment reads.

These scripts are not imported by the application entry. Some import core functions because they are clients of the same public data behavior. That direction lets command-line replay reuse the rules without putting Node APIs into browser modules.

## Application-level test support

`tests/browser-test.ts` adapts Node tests to Playwright, manages browsers and contexts, records runtime versions, gathers page errors and provides artifact paths. `tests/artifact-server.ts` serves the built HTML over loopback. `tests/game-fixture.ts` contains public-control setup helpers, disk URLs and completion helpers.

`tests/deal-oracle.ts` independently computes a specified deal with BigInt. `tests/focus-bounds.ts`, `tests/readability.ts`, `tests/accessibility-tree.ts` and `tests/ui-snapshot.ts` provide focused measurement or comparison support. They are tools used by journeys, not application modules.

The many `.e2e.test.ts` files are grouped by the observable behavior they examine: controls, input, play, persistence, snapshots, lifecycle, clock edges, layout, motion, artwork, status, accessibility, touch and zoom. [Test policy](test-policy.md) explains the runner and evidence boundaries instead of repeating every assertion here.

## Diagnostic entries and configured outputs

`art/index.html` and `art/face-sheet.tsx` form a separate face-sheet build with `art/face-sheet.css`. It imports the real card and design definitions to render every face at a controlled size. `vite.art.config.ts` writes this entry to `.art`.

`art/session/index.html` and `art/session/session-harness.tsx` form a separate lifecycle harness. It mounts `Game` beside an unmount button. `vite.session.config.ts` writes it to `.session`. The harness exists so the browser suite can measure cleanup rather than infer it from a page navigation.

The production build writes `dist/index.html`. Local dependencies live under `node_modules`; browser downloads, temporary browser files, npm cache and test work have separate ignored directories. `test-results` holds browser runtime and journey artifacts. These directories have operational roles but are not additional application source layers.

There is no generated route tree, backend, API client, asset service or utility framework to discover beyond this map. For command ordering see [Build pipeline](build-pipeline.md); for import and runtime separation see [React boundaries](react-boundaries.md).

import { generateBoard } from '../src/game/deck.ts';
import { PREFERENCES_KEY } from '../src/game/session/storage.ts';
import { TOURNAMENTS_KEY } from '../src/game/tournament/format.ts';
import { expect, test } from './browser-test.ts';
import { GAME_URL } from './game-fixture.ts';
import type { Page } from '@playwright/test';

const SAVED_PREFERENCES = JSON.stringify({
  schemaVersion: 1,
  size: 10,
  bestMoves: { '4': 8 },
});

test('four-player tournament reuses each match deal and saves its finished bracket', async ({
  page,
  gameURL,
}) => {
  await page.clock.install({ time: new Date('2026-01-01T00:00:00Z') });
  await page.addInitScript(({ key, value }) => localStorage.setItem(key, value), {
    key: PREFERENCES_KEY,
    value: SAVED_PREFERENCES,
  });
  await page.goto(gameURL || GAME_URL);
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Tournament', exact: true }).click();
  for (const [index, name] of ['Ada', 'Bo', 'Cora', 'Dev'].entries())
    await page.getByLabel(`Player ${index + 1}`, { exact: true }).fill(name);
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Start tournament', exact: true }).click();
  await page.clock.pauseAt(new Date('2026-01-01T00:01:00Z'));
  await expect(page.getByText('Round: Semifinal', { exact: true })).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.getByText('Now playing: Ada', { exact: true })).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.getByRole('columnheader', { name: 'Winner', exact: true })).toBeVisible();

  const firstCode = await matchCode(page, 0);
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Start turn', exact: true }).click();
  await expect(page.locator('.card')).toHaveCount(36);
  await finishTurn(page, firstCode);
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Next turn', exact: true }).click();
  await expect(page.getByText('Now playing: Dev', { exact: true })).toBeVisible();
  expect(await matchCode(page, 0)).toBe(firstCode);
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Start turn', exact: true }).click();
  await expect(page.locator('.card')).toHaveCount(36);
  await finishTurn(page, firstCode);
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Next match', exact: true }).click();

  const secondCode = await matchCode(page, 1);
  expect(secondCode).not.toBe(firstCode);
  await expect(page.getByText('Now playing: Bo', { exact: true })).toBeVisible();
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Start turn', exact: true }).click();
  await finishTurn(page, secondCode);
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Next turn', exact: true }).click();
  await expect(page.getByText('Now playing: Cora', { exact: true })).toBeVisible();
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Start turn', exact: true }).click();
  await finishTurn(page, secondCode);
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Next match', exact: true }).click();

  const finalCode = await matchCode(page, 2);
  expect(finalCode).not.toBe(firstCode);
  expect(finalCode).not.toBe(secondCode);
  await expect(page.getByText('Round: Final', { exact: true })).toBeVisible();
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Start turn', exact: true }).click();
  await expect(page.locator('.card')).toHaveCount(64);
  await finishTurn(page, finalCode);
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Next turn', exact: true }).click();
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Start turn', exact: true }).click();
  await finishTurn(page, finalCode);
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Champion: Ada', exact: true })).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Back to game', exact: true })).toBeVisible();

  expect(await page.evaluate((key) => localStorage.getItem(key), PREFERENCES_KEY)).toBe(
    SAVED_PREFERENCES,
  );
  const history = await page.evaluate((key) => localStorage.getItem(key), TOURNAMENTS_KEY);
  expect(history).not.toBeNull();
  expect(JSON.parse(history ?? '{}').tournaments).toHaveLength(1);
  await page.reload();
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Tournament', exact: true }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Past tournaments', exact: true })).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.locator('.past-tournament-list summary')).toContainText('Champion: Ada');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Export tournament', exact: true }).click();
  const exported = JSON.parse(
    await page.getByLabel('Tournament JSON', { exact: true }).inputValue(),
  );
  expect(exported.data.phase).toBe('finished');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Load tournament', exact: true }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Champion: Ada', exact: true })).toBeVisible();
});

test('eight-player setup seeds the documented opening match and Leave tournament returns to play', async ({
  page,
  gameURL,
}) => {
  await page.goto(gameURL);
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Tournament', exact: true }).click();
  await page.getByLabel('Players', { exact: true }).selectOption('8');
  for (let index = 0; index < 8; index += 1)
    await page.getByLabel(`Player ${index + 1}`, { exact: true }).fill(`P${index + 1}`);
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Start tournament', exact: true }).click();
  await expect(page.getByText('Round: Quarterfinal', { exact: true })).toBeVisible();
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Export tournament', exact: true }).click();
  const exported = JSON.parse(
    await page.getByLabel('Tournament JSON', { exact: true }).inputValue(),
  );
  expect(exported.data.matches[0].playerSeeds).toEqual([1, 8]);
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Start turn', exact: true }).click();
  await expect(page.locator('.card')).toHaveCount(16);
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Leave tournament', exact: true }).click();
  await expect(page.locator('.card')).toHaveCount(100);
  expect(await page.evaluate((key) => localStorage.getItem(key), TOURNAMENTS_KEY)).toBeNull();
});

async function matchCode(page: Page, index: number): Promise<string> {
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Export tournament', exact: true }).click();
  const value: unknown = JSON.parse(
    await page.getByLabel('Tournament JSON', { exact: true }).inputValue(),
  );
  if (!value || typeof value !== 'object' || !('data' in value))
    throw new Error('No tournament data.');
  const data = value.data;
  if (!data || typeof data !== 'object' || !('matches' in data) || !Array.isArray(data.matches))
    throw new Error('No bracket matches.');
  const match: unknown = data.matches[index];
  if (
    !match ||
    typeof match !== 'object' ||
    !('boardCode' in match) ||
    typeof match.boardCode !== 'string'
  )
    throw new Error('Missing match deal code.');
  return match.boardCode;
}

async function finishTurn(page: Page, code: string): Promise<void> {
  const deck = generateBoard(code).deck;
  const first = new Map<number, number>();
  const pairs: [number, number][] = [];
  deck.forEach((face, index) => {
    const previous = first.get(face);
    if (previous === undefined) first.set(face, index);
    else pairs.push([previous, index]);
  });
  for (const [firstIndex, secondIndex] of pairs) {
    await page.locator('.card').nth(firstIndex).click();
    await page.locator('.card').nth(secondIndex).click();
  }
  await expect(page.locator('.card.matched')).toHaveCount(deck.length);
}
